speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That It is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, by way of a guarantee for bank loans made on or after the 15th day of November, 1955, and before the 1st day of June, 1956, for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver their grain; to provide also that the governor in council may extend the application of the act to cover loans made before the 1st day of June, 1957; and to provide further that any amount paid to a bank under the act be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Is there going to be an explanation of the resolution before we proceed with the discussion?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
The purpose of this bill is to provide a partial guarantee of loans made by the chartered banks to producers against grain on farms, and to reinforce the security that would ordinarily be available under the Bank Act.

Grain
costs would be paid either by the borrower directly when he obtained an advance, or indirectly as a deduction from his participation payment if the interest and administration costs were to be absorbed by the wheat board.
Advances by the wheat board mean that the board would use money realized from the sale of grain delivered by all producers to lend to certain producers. Inevitably there would be costs and losses. Costs which were not paid by the borrower and losses would be deducted from the proceeds of the sale of grain, and would ultimately come out of the pockets of those producers who either had not obtained advances or had repaid them. I do not believe that this should be done and I challenge any member from the wheat-growing areas of the prairies to defend such a proposal.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: We will debate that matter this morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Good; I love to debate with my hon. friend.
Our conclusion, therefore, was that the wheat board was not as well equipped as the banks to make loans, the costs to the borrower would not be less if the board made the loans, such lending would be a misuse of board funds, and the board itself would be permanently damaged if it were turned into a lending and collection agency.
If the wheat board, on the other hand, is not to use producers' money for the making of advances, then I see no argument at all why the board should get involved in the business. The banks have the resources and the lending experience, and they have the legal and constitutional right to take adequate security, which the wheat board does not have.
Some proposals have been made that the board should make interest-free advances. For the board to make interest-free advances and absorb the cost and the losses as a charge against producers' participation certificates would, as I have already said, be a gross misuse of board funds. For the board to advance moneys on behalf of the treasury and bear none of the costs or the losses is a different proposition. This means that the treasury would be asked to make loans without interest to all western producers against farm-stored grain whether or not they needed the advance. No other producer in Canada obtains such interest-free advances. Moreover, I do not think the taxpayer should be asked to make interest-free advances to producers which they could invest immediately, for example, in government bonds and earn a return of 3 per cent or so.

I shall not say much at this stage about the provisions of the bill itself. The limit on loans is $1,500 to an individual borrower, which is $500 more than in 1951. The interest rate is 5 per cent, down J per cent from 1951. This rate was negotiated between the banks and the Department of Finance. It is the same as under the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
The bank guarantee is a smaller proportion of total loans than in 1951, partly because of the limited loss experience under the previous legislation and partly because these loans are secured by farm stored grain, rather than standing crops. The guarantee will apply to loans made under the conditions laid down in the bill since November 15, 1955. The over-all limit on guaranteed loans is raised from $20 million to $50 million.
Security must be taken under section 88 of the Bank Act, and the bill provides that such security takes priority over other liens. The borrower is also required to assign one-half of the proceeds of future deliveries of grain to repayment of the loan. In the 1951 legislation the assignment covered the proceeds of all deliveries until full repayment.
In the event that elevator congestion prevails at the opening of next crop year, which is quite likely because of the big crop harvested in 1955, the bill provides that the guarantee can be extended to loans made under the same conditions between October 1, 1956 and June 1, 1957.
As hon. members are aware, the order paper contains notice of another bill by which it is proposed to relieve the wheat board of the cost of carrying excessive stocks of wheat accumulated as a result of nature's bounty during these past years. These two proposals, if accepted, will enable the board to follow an aggressive yet orderly marketing policy without fear that carrying charges will eat up the producers' equity in existing wheat board stocks, and will enable those producers who are short of cash to obtain temporary advances pending normal deliveries within the crop year.
They do not in any way alter the fundamental grain marketing policy of the government, which is to sell as much grain as possible at the best possible prices. That policy has been a remarkable success. It has moved enormous quantities of grain at reasonably good prices. In this period of temporary surpluses it has given a degree of stability to world markets that might otherwise have collapsed, as they did in the 1930's.
There are heavy stocks of wheat in Canada for one and only one reason-good rainfall on the prairies for several years. There has been no increase in acreage. There have been

no subsidies. Sales have been good, more than enough to clear out average crops. They continue to be good.
In the rest of the world stocks are also heavy, but for different reasons. In nearly all other parts of the world wheat production has been stimulated by price supports or by protective measures of one kind or another. We should all recognize, however, that the United States, which increased its acreage so sharply a few years ago, is now taking measures to bring its acreage back to more normal levels.
In these circumstances of heavy stocks throughout the world, the government and the wheat board face a difficult task in marketing Canadian wheat to best advantage. You will expect me to say that we are doing a good job. But I suggest to hon. members on the other side of the house that before they criticize the government's wheat policy, they take a good look at the facts, and consider the effect of their remarks upon the position of the Canadian wheat board as a marketing agency.
The great danger in the present situation is that sellers may be panicked into dumping stocks on to world markets that cannot absorb them. This is what happened in the early 1930's. It is in no one's interest to see this happen again.
In due course, if sensible policies are followed and uneconomic supports and barriers are removed, present excessive stocks will be absorbed. In the meantime it is encumbent upon all of us to have steady nerves and cool heads.
It seems to me that there should not be a prolonged debate on this legislation. The provisions of the bill have been in effect since November 15. We may as well face the fact that wheat board selling is no longer a dominant factor in the movement of this crop; the amount of grain that will be exported depends upon the ability of our railroads and our seaports to deliver that grain to ships.
The board has succeeded in its selling efforts in spite of the advice of opposition members. It has not reduced the price, as almost every Conservative newspaper in the country has demanded it should; it has not bartered its wheat for old bottles or anything of that sort; it has not exchanged its wheat for foreign currencies; it has not given wheat away. It has consistently followed wheat board policy which has been successful for many years and which has been successful recently; that is, to exchange Canadian wheat for Canadian dollars.
Therefore I think it should be no particular part of this debate to belabour the wheat board. The wheat board has done its job.
Grain
True, it had to wait until opposition members expounded their theories in the fall, since foreign buyers were afraid the board would believe some of the opposition members. Well, we did not; we just waited until normal trading conditions would return. We are now back in the wheat business, and this bill is needed to meet an immediate situation. I hope this bill will receive your favourable consideration.

Marketings from prairie farms during the weei ending July 11 were approximately half at 4,770,00( bushels versus 8,656,000 bushels.

That is not a statement by members of the opposition; that is not a statement by those whom the minister seeks to chastise for any attempt to place these facts before the public. That is a statement by a bureau which was set up by the minister's own department to give the public the facts.
When we are told about sales for export and the fact that all is well, that the only concern now is in regard to the ability of the railway companies to deal with this problem, again we have the statement of the bureau of statistics which shows that for the last four weeks there has been a substantial reduction in export clearances. speechtext: How many weeks?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
That is for the four-week period. There was actually an improvement in the last of those four weeks, but the total for the four-week period shows a substantial reduction in export clearances, and certainly there is nothing to justify the optimistic statement that only the ability of the railways to handle the wheat can cause any concern about this situation.
Then we had the peculiarly reminiscent statement by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce that they had to wait until the members of the opposition expounded their theories last fall before this subject actually came forward for consideration. We were told also that this was likely to cause alarm, that this was likely to cause panic, that this was likely to disturb possible purchasers of our wheat. It is not within the rules of this house that I should use appropriate terms to describe a statement such is that made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this respect.
After all, this subject has been under dis-:ussion before. It has been pointed out in his house on a number of occasions that 'or several years the request has been made hat legislation be placed on the statute cooks so that when the situation required it, :ash advances could be made in respect of arm-stored grain. This is not something lew. I pointed out in the debate on the ipeech from the throne only two weeks ago hat in December, 1952, I had urged that we lave legislation on the statute books to deal vith cash payments in respect of farm-tored grain where that became necessary. 
This is not something new; this is not something which has emerged during the last few months. It is something, however, which has emerged in an acute form, not because of anything said by the opposition, not because of the bountiful crop alone, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce implies, but because wheat is piled on the farms of western Canada in unprecedented quantities and the farmers do not know where to get money for their immediate needs.
We come to the statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the government looked into the various methods which might be employed, and having decided that this must be dealt with by way of loan, it then decided that it should be done through the banks. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said this is not something that would be appropriate for the wheat board. I would point out that we have emphasized since long before this house sat, and have emphasized on every possible occasion since this became an acute problem, that we believed there were special circumstances to support the proposition that the only effective way in which this situation could be met would be to make cash advances through the wheat board on farm-stored grain in relation to an established quota, as has been done in regard to grain delivered in the past; and that this payment should be made in the ordinary way on the basis of the initial price fixed by the board, as an ordinary cash advance, as though the grain to that amount had already become the property of the board.
That would avoid any question about loans by the banks, the involved procedure which has been set up and the difficulties encountered by many farmers in actually even making arrangements to attend at the bank for this purpose.
The question is not one as between loans by the banks and loans by the wheat board. The question is between cash advances on farm-stored grain and a method of loan which does not satisfactorily meet the situation. That is the real issue. That has been the clear issue at all times; it is the issue now, and it is the issue which I would hope the government would still consider in its proper light.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has made a peculiarly interesting observation which I hope will not be overlooked in its implications. In explaining why he did not think the wheat board should be put in the position of being responsible for dealing with this problem, he said, and I believe I quote his words with accuracy, "I do not think that it"-that is, the wheat board-"would welcome producers shopping around amongst them for advances."

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: If that is the case the Minister of Trade and Commerce is simply saying that if the wheat board, through its agencies, were to make arrangements of this kind, the agencies, which the minister has now defined as the wheat elevator operators, would not welcome producers shopping around among them for advances. What does he mean by that? Either there would be a clear basis for advances or there would not. Is the minister implying that this would involve some improper procedure?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: You just do not understand the country elevator business.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
One thing that is perfectly certain is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce does not understand the problem he is dealing with, to judge from what he has said here this morning. He has directed all his remarks with a paternal sense of pain for the ignorance of the members of the opposition, without any regard to the fact that what has been asked and what we are asking is what the farmers of western Canada have been asking vigorously and in no uncertain terms for some considerable time.
When the Minister of Trade and Commerce warns us of the dire consequences that might come from the discussion of this subject in this house, does he suggest for one moment that the people he thinks might become alarmed do not read our newspapers and do not read the statements made by our farmers? Or when he singles out what he describes as the Conservative press, I wonder if he now includes in that expression the Winnipeg Free Press, which has given no uncertain expression to its demands that some alternative method be employed. Certainly the Winnipeg Free Press is not hesitant in criticizing the government's handling of its wheat policy. Certainly the Winnipeg Free Press has not been reluctant to point out that there is a crisis. I would point out also that there are other newspapers in western Canada which have been equally vocal and equally vigorous and which, with the optimistic approach to the general subject which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has injected into his remarks, I would not previously have described as Conservative newspapers.
No; this subject is one that has been placed before the people of this country and before any possible purchasers of our wheat by the farmers themselves, by their representative organizations and by the general discussions which have taken place. As a matter of fact
the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) is quite aware that he did not have to wait until he came into the House of Commons to learn that there are certain strong views expressed on this subject. I feel sure that is true also of other hon. members. The Minister of Justice has indicated that he welcomed the frank discussion of this subject and the way it came forward. We all have occasions when discussions of a similarly frank nature take place, but most certainly the Minister of Justice is under no illusion that this is the only place where this subject has been brought forward for consideration, and where the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the operations of the government in this matter have been subjected to some substantial measure of criticism.
The figures from the dominion bureau of statistics, to which I have just referred, show that during the past four weeks farm sales are down and export clearances are down. As I quite clearly stated, one out of those four weeks, the last one, did show an improvement; nevertheless the total for the four weeks is down. There is certainly nothing in those statistics issued by the bureau, which is in the department of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that justifies in any way the broad and optimistic statements he has made.
There are other reasons why this problem should be discussed and should be tackled. This loan system is not one which the Minister of Trade and Commerce expects to be employed to any considerable extent. Once again, having regard to the context of his remarks, may I point out that he implies that the government was considering some arrangements to meet the situation which responsible newspapers in western Canada described as a crisis, and which farm organizations have definitely asked everyone in Canada to recognize as a crisis.
If that is so, then let us consider the attitude of the responsible minister, as stated in his own words. In Calgary on November 28, in referring to this loan plan, the Minister of Trade and Commerce used these words:
It is my hope and belief that comparatively little use will be made of the lending facilities, that most farmers are either in a position to carry on without borrowing or are in a position to finance in the ordinary way.
Those words are clear. The Minister of Trade and Commerce simply does not regard this as legislation designed to meet any real emergency. He is looking on it as something that will not be used extensively. The farmers of western Canada have made it clear through statements they have made within their organizations and individually that they

Grain
do regard it as a crisis and that they do regard some solution of the problem as urgent and immediate. For that reason the proposal before us is not adequate.
I wish to make it clear at this point, Mr. Chairman, that we will not vote against the resolution. Inadequate though it may be, unsatisfactory though it may be, with interest rates on the basis they are to be charged under this plan, we are not going to seek to deny whatever relief may be afforded by this method. We believe it is appropriate, however, to point out that this does not meet the situation. We do point out the situation to the government once again, and we urge them to reconsider their position. We believe that whether or not this legislation is passed the government should reconsider the justification for making cash advances on farm-stored grain.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce made the statement that no other producers in Canada would receive similar consideration. One thing, Mr. Chairman, perhaps not recognized fully by many people in other parts of Canada who live outside the prairie provinces is that no other producers in Canada are in exactly the same position. We are fully aware of the fact that other agricultural producers have problems that they think are just as critical, in some cases more critical. I would point out that the potato grower on his farm in northern New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island faces an even more urgent problem. He has a crop that cannot be kept. It is a perishable crop. The same is true of the fruit growers in the Annapolis valley and elsewhere. They have perishable crops that cannot be stored. The problem they face on their own farms is even more critical because, with all the difficulties facing the wheat growers, the growers of potatoes, apples and other products of that kind cannot keep those products against the day when there may be some return.
Nevertheless there is a difference in this problem and one that I think the potato grower, the apple grower and other agricultural producers in other parts of Canada will recognize. By law the wheat producers of western Canada are unable to sell to anyone but the government agency. That is the key to the whole nature of this special problem. We also must recognize the scale of the problem from the point of view of Canada as a whole. Nearly one billion bushels of wheat are involved in the consideration of this problem. That involves an enormous amount of money for all Canadians, and it is not only a problem of the individual wheat producer,

critical though his problem may be. This is a problem affecting the whole of Canada.
We are also confronted with the fact that the wheat producers, who under legal restrictions are not permitted to sell to any but the government agency, have on their farms at this time nearly 500 million bushels of wheat. An enormous percentage of the world's available wheat supply is lying on the farms of western Canada at this time, or is contained in some sort of temporary shelter. That is the problem. One of the things which should be borne in mind, without in any way debating all the questions that may arise as to details of operation and otherwise, is the fact that the government says by law "this is our grain", which makes them in effect the owners of that grain the moment it is harvested.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: They cannot sell it to anybody else.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I emphasize that point. In effect the moment the wheat is harvested the government becomes the owner of the grain. There is no other purchaser. The wheat farmer has been permitted to assume, and with reason, that the wheat would be taken up appropriately year by year so that from this grain, which must be delivered to the government agency, he would get an adequate return on the basis of a quota per acre at the initial price fixed by the board, and that this amount would then be handed to him as a cash advance on his quota book.
Our argument, and we have put it forward for some considerable time, not just in the last few months, is that the government alone can take the wheat and the government is already in fact the ultimate owner and by law can be the only owner in the end when it is sold. Therefore where the wheat cannot be taken into the elevators and the farmers need this money for their immediate requirements, then on that wheat, which in effect belongs to the government, the farmers should be able to go in the usual way and get a cash advance on a proper quota basis at the regular initial price, such advance to be marked on their quota book, with the understanding and the undertaking that that amount of grain will be delivered to the elevator on demand the moment they receive notice that the space is available.
Surely there is nothing complicated about that. The ordinary machinery now existing would carry this out without any problem of any kind. There would be none of this ominous shopping around that the Minister of Trade and Commerce implies. Perhaps his mind is accustomed to shopping around for a consideration. The fact remains, however,

that this system is one which involves no shopping around. This system is one which would be on a clear and understandable basis, with the cash payment entered in the quota book in the ordinary way and paid to the farmer.
That, Mr. Chairman, is what we ask. We certainly will support the resolution, inadequate though it may be to meet the problems facing the farmers; and though we are told that it will contain provisions which in themselves we think are onerous and unfair certainly it is better than nothing. We do urge, however, that with the adoption of legislation of this kind the government does not make the mistake of thinking it has dealt with the problem. I hope it will look at the statements that are appearing in the press of western Canada and those coming from farm organizations before the childish threat is issued to this house that we are in some danger of creating a panic if we even dare to discuss problems for which we are responsible. May I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Just talk to the chairman.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
-that even if his Liberal supporters are prepared to applaud that kind of dictatorial statement, he is not going to find any acceptance of warnings of that kind here in the House of Commons. This is still a free House of Commons, and we are going to carry out our obligations in the house. Certainly there is no greater obligation than to point out to the government that along with any arrangement of this kind there should go further consideration of a simple and practical method by which the farmers can receive some cash immediately without any involved procedure in return for wheat which in effect already belongs to the government and to no one else. Since it does belong to the government and since the farmer himself certainly can exercise no control over the availability of freight cars and elevator space, there should be no interest on payments made in respect of advances on the wheat which the government has already in effect taken under its control.
That is a proposition which emerges naturally and logically from the position the government has taken. I hope all our friends in every part of the house who have had reason to give this subject consideration will let us have the advantage of their opinions, because we are not merely dealing with the motion concerning this resolution now before us. In this discussion we have an opportunity once again to urge the government to give consideration to the only practical proposition that has been put forward to give
Grain
the farmer some relief in the critical situation in which he now finds himself. We know perfectly well that there have been bountiful crops. Of course there have been such crops. By that statement the Minister of Trade and Commerce would seem to imply that our only hope is to have a disastrous crop failure. That is what in effect is implicit in that statement. The only suggestion they have to offer is a disaster of another kind.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Balderdash.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I am glad to know there is at least one Liberal member who is willing to have his voice heard. All I hope is that, instead of the kind of comment that has just been made, some Liberal members opposite will show that they are prepared to discuss this subject during the debate in spite of the admonition which has been given to them by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: They will not say anything.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is always reason for
hope. We might hope that some of the things which are now being said privately will be said publicly by hon. members opposite with regard to this subject.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: They will not even deny what you are saying.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is true that
there have been wonderful crops. Surely, however, this government is not going to just leave the impression that all it intends to do is wait for bad crops to solve this problem. If this situation were as simple, as easy and as good as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has implied by his recent remarks, may I ask this question: Why was he complaining about the action of the United States government? If there is no reason for concern about what has been done, why did he make a public statement about the action of the United States government with regard to sales which he thought might conceivably disturb these operations?
The fact is that he was concerned about it, in spite of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture apparently thought surpluses were a good thing. He was disturbed about it and he said so. I only wish that in this discussion this morning something of that concern had found its way into his remarks, so there might have been some real relationship between what he said and the situation as it actually exists.
Whatever the situation is, Mr. Chairman, there is one other consideration that has not been met by the government. The Minister of Trade and Commerce made the statement that we would find in the speech from the

Grain
throne the whole wheat policy of the government. This morning we had been left with the clear impression that the government has no other thought with regard to this matter except what is found in this resolution.
Let us remember what the minister said. He told us that there have been good crops; that this is the only reason there has been any serious problem; and that there have been, of course, some difficulties with regard to the availability of cars. We know that within recent weeks ships have been lying at anchor in the harbour at Vancouver, unable to pick up the grain which they were ready to move. It is explained that this situation might be the result of the failure to get wheat there because of the shortage of box cars. There is also the statement-and it has not been satisfactorily challenged in any way-that there is over 100 million bushels of storage space not being used in the elevators of this country at the present time.	*
The farmers of Canada are not responsible for that situation. The farmers of Canada have in their hands no power to deal with the problem of the availability of freight cars and other means of transportation. That matter is in the hands of the government alone. The farmers of western Canada, who are in a unique position because of what I have already pointed out, should be told at this time what the plan of the government is for the current year. In addition to anything that is said in relation to this resolution, surely this is the time for the farmers of western Canada, who are in that special position, to foe told what the policies of the government are in relation to the crop for the coming year; that is, for this present year. If they do not know, how can they possibly make their plans for the seeding which will take place in the not too distant future? The farmers have a right to know what is going to happen next fall. They have a right to know what this government intends to do if we have another bumper crop, as might reasonably be expected with the amount of precipitation there has been during this winter. No matter how inadequate this legislation may be, and even though they have not yet agreed to provide for cash advances on farm-stored grain, certainly the government should come forward with a clear statement of policy so the farmers may be able to make their plans for this year with some knowledge of what they may reasonably expect. Otherwise the only hope that is offered to them is disaster of another kind. No solution of the problem is offered to them by this government except the possibility that there will be a disastrous crop failure. Surely they are entitled to more than that.

I therefore close these remarks, Mr. Chairman, with the statement that in supporting this resolution we do so simply because we would not wish to urge that any relief, however limited or unsatisfactory it may be, should be denied to any farmer who wishes to avail himself of it. At the same time, however, we urge that the government reconsider its position and decide to make cash advances on farm-stored grain by the method and for the reasons I have outlined. We also urge that before these discussions are closed, the government make an announcement to this house and, through this house and the press gallery in the house as well as through Hansard, to the country, inform the farmers in the three prairie provinces what they may expect next fall in relation to the crop that will be grown this year.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The resolution the Minister of Trade and Commerce has presented to parliament at this time to meet the severe shortage of cash on the prairies is probably the most unpopular move this government has made in the realm of agricultural policy since October, 1947, when the ceilings were taken off oats and barley and then were placed back on the grain exchange.
This morning we have been read a lecture by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He has suggested to us that we should curtail the debate, that we should not speak in this debate, that we should not discuss the serious position of the western farmers. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is again up to his old tricks. He is trying to muzzle parliament and prevent free discussion. This government is a past master at muzzling parliament. Yesterday we had a fine example of the way in which this government treats parliament and the members of the House of Commons. Yesterday I had before the house a bill proposing a reduction in interest rates on small loans.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I think the hon. member will agree that neither a reflection on a vote of the house nor the discussion of an alternative measure is in order under this resolution, on which we are allowing wide discussion of the farmers' problems.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not commenting on a vote of the house at all. I am commenting on the attitude of this government. When a member of the opposition has a proposal before this house, not necessarily yesterday but any time in the past, that might embarrass the government, what does the government do? It has somebody stand up and move the adjournment of the debate, using its parliamentary majority to cut off debate and kill

the discussion. Then when the adjournment cannot be moved because it is a piece of government legislation that is highly unpopular, as this legislation before us now is, of course the minister uses veiled threats to attempt to accomplish the same result.
The minister and the Liberal party stand alone in saying to the people of western Canada that the legislation now before this house will solve the problem. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is smarting under the treatment he received within the last few months in western Canada. He went to speak to one farm convention after another to try to ram down the throats of the farmers this same kind of garbage he is attempting to ram down our throats this morning. At these conventions the farmers repudiated the minister and said, "We are not supporting bank loans; we are, in fact, opposing bank loans." Then this morning the minister makes the utterly ridiculous statement that anyone who is against this legislation; anyone who says that bank loans are not good; anyone who says that the wheat board should be instrumental in making advances to the farther, is against the wheat board.
That is a fine statement to make regarding the Saskatchewan wheat pool delegates, who on November 1 last at the opening of their annual meeting passed an emergency motion asking for cash advances through elevator companies on farm-stored grain. No organization has promoted the wheat board method of marketing more than the Saskatchewan wheat pool. I am sure the delegates at that meeting proposed something they thought would help the wheat board and would not, in fact, hinder it in any way.
When the minister threatens parliament and tries to choke off discussion, he does not stop with threatening the opposition, as the Leader of the Opposition said, he manhandles the Liberal party back benchers and says, "Fellows, toe the line". He says there are people in this country opposed to the wheat board. Yes, there are. Every time you hear anybody say there is widespread opposition in Canada to the wheat board, you can bet your bottom dollar it is a member of the Liberal party who is sowing the seeds of opposition to the wheat board.
That is not all that is wrong with this legislation. The minister has contempt for the opposition, he has contempt for his own party, and he has contempt for parliament. I was surprised that the Leader of the Opposition should overlook the very important point that this legislation in fact came into effect on November 15. Now, months later, parliament is being asked to rubber stamp something the government put into effect months 67509-39J
Grain
ago. You know how it was put into effect? The Minister of Trade and Commerce is quite agile at a lot of things. He was in Regina addressing the wheat pool convention on November 5, I believe. It was there he made the big announcement of this bank loan legislation. Parliament was not in session; parliament in the minister's opinion did not have to be called into session. All the Minister of Trade and Commerce had to do was to stage a radio-T.V. show and announce the policy. He did not need parliament. The announcement was made in that way, and months later parliament is called and we are asked to rubber stamp this legislation the government is proposing.
As I have said, not since 1947 has this government done anything in connection with prairie farm matters that was so thoroughly and so unanimously unpopular as is this measure. The prairie producers resent having this bitter pill of bank loans rammed down their throats. It is no alternative to a system of cash advances. It is not working, and was not supposed to work. The minister said it is not going to be used very much, and it is not. Not many farmers can get a loan. This method was not used much in
1951.
The Leader of the Opposition said the position of his party has been clear since
1952.	The position of the C.C.F. was clear for many years prior to that. In 1942-43 the members of this group were advocating cash advances. On December 3, 1951, we presented a motion requesting cash advances. The situation then was not nearly as critical as it is now. At that time the government put through parliament somewhat similar legislation guaranteeing bank loans up to $20 million. As the minister well knows, just a little over $600,000 of the $20 million was actually used.
I have in my hands figures showing the bank loans that have been obtained in the first two weeks of the operation of this act. Some hon. members may think that if the act is going to remain in effect for some months, it would be used very little in the first two weeks. The fact of the matter is that many farmers who felt they were in such a desperate financial position that they were forced, because of circumstances, to go to the bank to ask for a loan would do so in the early part of the operation of the act. I have the figures for the first two weeks of the operation of this act. In that time there was loaned to less than 3,000 farmers, out of 200,000 producers on the prairies, just over $2-5 million. That is an indication not only that the legislation is faulty, not only that the banks are exceedingly careful in

Grain
making these loans and are endeavouring to make as tew loans as possible, but that the producers themselves are not anxious to have this kind of loan.
The producer believes that he is forced to go to the bank to ask for loan on his summer's work, a loan on his wheat, a loan on something which is his cash asset, and worse still is forced to pay interest on it. He is, in fact, paying interest on his own income. How many times have I heard farmers say, "We would like to get the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this position, where at the end of each month instead of getting his regular cheque he would be told that legislation was being provided whereby he could go to the bank and borrow his month's wages, go into debt and pay interest on his own money." That is the basic reason that wheat producers are opposed to this legislation.
It will not work for a great many reasons. It will not work because it is probably correct to say that a very large percentage of western farmers do not go to banks, do not do ordinary banking business. As a matter of fact there are more credit unions in Saskatchewan than there are branches of chartered banks in that province. Most of these credit unions are doing business in the rural areas, so that a great proportion of the prairie farmers never darken a bank door. In many instances they do not know the bank managers, and they may have to travel 40 or 50 miles to find a branch of a chartered bank. They go into a bank to see the manager, and the farmer is a total stranger. The banker cannot tell if he is a farmer; cannot tell if he has a quarter section or six quarter sections. The bank manager cannot tell whether he has 1,000 bushels of wheat, 10,000 bushels or none. The bank manager is placed in an untenable position. The bank manager is just as much opposed to this legislation as the producer who is forced to go to the bank and ask for a loan.
The principle of forcing farmers to pay interest on their own money would have been just as bad if the government had included the credit unions in this proposal. I do not know why the government would not allow the credit unions to have the same privileges and the same guarantee as the banks. The farmers who do business with the credit unions would certainly be a lot happier to go to the credit union manager, who knows their circumstances, to ask for a loan under this legislation. The government, of course, are friendly with the banks. They know the heads of the banks. The government and the banks are very close. However, the government will not tolerate

guarantees for the credit unions to allow them to compete with the banks for banking business on equal terms.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Surely.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Does the hon. member know that in the case of fishermen the banks and credit unions are on the same footing as far as loans are concerned?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, that is the toe in the door. It has taken a long time to correct that situation, and I am glad the government made the change, though it still has a long way to go. It took private members to suggest it; it was not a government idea. I am suggesting now that the credit unions be given precisely the same guarantee as was given to the banks, and I am willing at this time to stake my reputation on the statement that on loans the credit unions make to purchasers they will come to the government for a smaller guarantee and a smaller recompense than in the case of the banks, because the records of credit unions show that they have sustained very few, almost negligible losses in the business they do.
This legislation is wholly inadequate because of the total amount of money farmers can obtain under it. It is bad enough for the farmers to have no money and to have a lot of wheat in their yards they cannot sell. It is bad enough that the farmers owe money all around town; but it is even more serious for the local merchants, the storekeepers, garage men, implement dealers and oil dealers who have not just one set of accounts but have the accounts of perhaps 50 or 100 farmers to worry about. It is the local merchants in the prairie provinces who are carrying the load. They have carried it in the past and they are carrying it today. That is why the resolutions which came to the government were so unanimously in favour of cash advances; the storekeepers and merchants wanted some measure which would enable the farmers to pay their accounts.
The minister informed us yesterday that he has thousands of pieces of paper in his possession respecting a return I asked for in relation to the production of papers in regard to cash advances. I am positive that fewer than 1 per cent, if indeed any, of the resolutions or letters from wheat producers in the minister's possession state that they are in favour of the policy that is now being presented to parliament. The producers are almost unanimously opposed to this method of handling the situation at this time.

The government is proposing this kind of legislation as a means of dealing with the problem. It is proposing other legislation which asks parliament to approve the payment of storage on excess carryover. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that the people of Canada, the taxpayers, would resent having to provide the money necessary to pay interest-free cash advances. I do not believe that statement. I do not think it is true because I believe, although I could be wrong, that the four parties in this house will give unanimous approval to the government's proposition that parliament and the national treasury should meet the cost of storage and carrying charges on wheat.
I am just as convinced that had the government had the foresight, courage and imagination to bring in a proposal for cash advances, there would be the same unanimous support in this house as is now likely to be given to the storage provision.
I suggest that the government should do one more thing and should do it now. The government should not make an interim payment on the 1954 wheat crop and then a final payment some months later. I do not think that is the best method of handling the situation at this time, when a severe shortage of cash exists. I believe that the government through the governor in council should now close out the wheat board account for 1954-55. The inventory should be valued at present sale prices, and the farmers at this time should ge given the largest payment that can be made out of the funds that happen to be in that account after it is closed out. They should not receive a small payment now and a small payment some months later, with all the extra cost that is involved in the wheat board making a separate payment.
I would hope that under the legislation now before the house the payment could be more than the 15 cents a bushel which was paid last year in the form of an interim and final payment. I would hope that legislation before the house would make it possible for the government to make a payment of 20 cents or even 25 cents a bushel. Certainly the account should be closed out and the farmers should be paid that money as soon as possible.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said that the only danger which threatened wheat markets in the last few months has been speeches by members of parliament. I presume he means speeches by hon. members who have been talking about cash advances. I also presume he means that the wheat pool officials are damaging the grain business when they go about and ask for cash advances. The minister rose and said the other day the
Grain
United States is to blame. It is the United States policy which is to blame, he says. He says that bartering and accepting legal currency and gifts will not be sufficient to increase our sales, but the United States is following that policy and is increasing its sales and distribution to a large extent.
I was pleased at the announcement that a trade delegation from the U.S.S.R. is coming to Ottawa. It would be my hope that the minister himself would handle the deliberations of that conference, and that the government would face the export situation with an open mind. I hope the government will be prepared to undertake any financial steps that may be necessary to enable the export of Canadian wheat, and to enable sales to be made.
The minister does not like the word barter. I would suggest that the minister make contract sales, if he does not want to use the term barter and in attempting to sell wheat, be prepared to sell it to nations behind the iron curtain or to any other nation. The government should be prepared to make those sales where necessary on a contract basis over a number of years; and where credit extension may be necessary, the government should not stop at one year but extend credits over two, three or four years if necessary and if such credits will result in an expansion of our wheat trade.
Some announcements concerning export sales that have been made in the past month have given some encouragement to the farmers. These announcements relate almost entirely to sales of Canadian wheat to countries behind the iron curtain. It is not an accident that these sales are to communist countries. The reason that sales of wheat to countries behind the iron curtain are the main hope for increased sales of Canadian wheat at this time is the fact that public law No. 480, under which the United States congress is supporting and promoting the disposal of United States wheat, confines the disposal of such wheat to countries other than those behind the iron curtain.
I think that Canada should be in the position of promoting sales to any country in the world and by whatever method might be necessary, including the methods that are being used in the United States. We should not have lagged behind the United States and have reached the position where today apparently our only substantial hope for increased sales appears to be countries behind the iron curtain.
We have this legislation before the house, and it is most unpopular. As I have said, no

Grain
one is in favour of it except the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his supporters. They are endeavouring to drag in the farm organizations and show that they are in support of this policy. The provincial leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan made a similar statement early in November, and an official reply had to be issued by the Saskatchewan wheat pool denying that they were in favour of bank loans. In part that statement had this to say:
The policy of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, as approved by its delegates in annual meeting, is clear-cut. It does not favour the government's proposal for bank loans. It firmly believes that the conditions are such that extraordinary measures are called for, and that these should include advances against farm-stored grain, and that such advances should be made to individual farmers through elevator companies in accordance with an agreement between the companies and the wheat board.
The minister attempts to show that when we support having the wheat board make these arrangements, we want the wheat board itself to go out and make the loans. Nothing could be further from the truth. All we are asking is that the wheat board make the arrangements whereby the grain elevator companies can make the advances. The elevator company agents are in a much better position to make advances than are the banks. I have said that we have more credit unions in Saskatchewan than branches of the chartered banks, and I would say that there are 12 elevator agents in Saskatchewan for every branch of a chartered bank.
The elevator agent is personally acquainted with the farmer. He knows the farmer's business, because he is a close friend of the farmer who brings grain to his elevator. Most likely he knows the amount of grain the farmer has on his farm. He is in position to make the advance. Why does the minister say the government will not do it through the elevator companies? His claim and he is wrong again is that the elevator company or the wheat board cannot be given the power to place a lien against the grain of the type which a chartered bank could obtain under the Bank Act.
The minister made another amazing statement the other day. He said it would be very risky for loans to be made by the elevator companies to farmers. Why? Because he said the farmer might feed the grain, the farmer might sell it to his neighbour or the farmer might not repay the loan. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was saying in effect that he could not support advances to farmers through the wheat board and the elevator system because the farmers are dishonest, because they are

likely to feed their own grain or because they are likely to sell it to their neighbours. I think that was a shameful statement, and it is a statement which the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Liberal party will not be allowed to forget.
I do not think the farmers of western Canada as a group are any more dishonest than any other group in Canada. I believe the western wheat producers are honest. The experience of the government under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, whereby the government has had to pay just 1/35 of 1 per cent of the money advanced under the act, shows that an overwhelming majority of prairie producers are wholly and completely honest. I believe that cash advances are practical and would be repaid almost without exception, and would give the government a cheaper method of making money available to the producers than the method now used.
If the farmers were given cash advances and the interest paid by the government it would cost the treasury 4 per cent on an advance of 90 cents per bushel, which is the most that has been asked and which is the amount the CCF is asking for. That would cost the federal treasury less than 4 cents per year to finance a bushel of wheat in the farmer's possession. The minister says we should not ask the taxpayer to do that, but according to the other resolution on the order paper-I want to say I am pleased it is there, and I am going to support it- the government and the taxpayer will assume carrying charges and storage charges on grain held by the wheat board in excess of 178 million bushels. What does that mean? It means 4 per cent on the whole initial price.

I suggest to the government that even at this late date it should withdraw this legislation and provide for cash advances, which would give the farmer in Canada at least part of that which is given to the producer in the United States. The farmer in the country immediately to the south is able to get $2.08 per bushel on 95 per cent of all the wheat he has harvested, with the advance being interest-free on delivery of the grain. If the United States government can provide a cash advance of $2.08 per bushel, surely this government should do more for the Canadian wheat producer than is being provided by this legislation, which attempts to shackle him with further interest charges.

Mr. Chairman, I think the question of bank loans against grain stored on the farm must be viewed in the light of present conditions, as well as in the light of the situation that existed at the time this policy was first put into effect by the government.
The minister stresses the fact that sales of wheat are picking up, that there is really no great marketing problem today, that the problem is rather a question of transportation and the lack of box cars. It is interesting to note that, because last year the farmers were told that it was not a problem of transportation but rather a lack of orders, that the elevators could not get orders. Now the farmers are told that there are plenty of orders but they cannot get box cars. Many farmers are beginning to wonder whether or not the railways are putting on a sit-down strike as a protest against the Crowsnest pass rates.
Be that as it may, the important point to note is that we are now approaching the end of the sixth month of the present crop year. It is ten months since the first costs were incurred in the production of this wheat, and it is over three months since harvesting operations were completed. In spite of that fact, there are many points in western Canada where farmers today are not able to deliver one single bushel of wheat against even a one-bushel quota. That is the situation that exists today, and that is why it is still very critical in so far as many points in western Canada are concerned.
In addition to that situation, there are amounts of wheat from previous crop years that are still being stored. Costs were incurred in the production of that wheat, and farmers are most desirous of being able to liquidate some of those costs. Those costs can be liquidated only by the sale of the wheat. Apparently the minister keeps forgetting that the production of wheat is not a costless thing. He seems to think that if the farmer has some wheat on his farm he can sell it and invest the proceeds in government bonds. Unfortunately that is not the
Grain
case at all. In a majority of cases the larger percentage of the wheat on the farm is already pledged, and the minister should keep that fact in mind.
The answer given by the government last fall that there would be bank loans against wheat stored on the farm caused a wave of protest meetings throughout western Canada.
I know that the minister has stated that those meetings were largely at the instigation either of the grain exchange or of certain interests in the large cities.
That may be true in certain parts of western Canada. I am not in a position to say whether it is or not. I can say that there is not one word of truth in that charge as far as my constituency is concerned. The protest meetings originated among the farmers themselves. You might say it was a spontaneous action on the part of the farmers, and generally a member of a local farmers' union would take the responsibility for first trying to arrange a meeting.
I was not in my constituency at the time the question came up, but I very soon received a long distance telephone call asking me to come down and attend some of the meetings. I would like to say that those meetings were not political in any shape or form. I did not go on the platform, but merely sat with the rest of the farmers. As a matter of fact there was no platform speaker. The meeting was called to order and the chairman was appointed, and then there was a free for all discussion. The discussion first of all took place on the government's proposal, because at that time it was merely a proposal, to make bank loans available to farmers against wheat in storage. I can say that there was very bitter protest against that suggestion.
I remember the first meeting. A resolution was moved that the farmers were unalterably opposed to such a suggestion. A good deal of discussion took place on that motion, but finally some farmers pointed out that whilst the majority were very much opposed to that proposal, nevertheless there were some farmers in such dire straits that they would have to take advantage of some form of loan. If they could not get what they wanted through advances they had better have the loans as suggested by the government, but they were prepared to take them against their better judgment.
The reason they opposed loans was largely that there are very large stocks of wheat on the farms and a very large percentage of those stocks are already pledged. That is something the minister does not appear to be able to get into his head. He has an idea that so long as the farmers can sell a small

May I ask the
hon. member a question? If the wheat is already pledged, is he suggesting that the government should make an advance on it just the same?

No, not on the 60 per cent of the wheat that is pledged. The government could certainly make an advance on the remaining 40 per cent at least, or it could make an advance on 50 per cent with the stipulation that a certain amount be used to pay off the obligations that have already been incurred. The reason such a large percentage of that wheat has already been pledged is that heavy costs were incurred in the production of the wheat. Farmers were obliged to get bank loans to meet those costs, and they were obliged to charge bills with machine companies, stores and oil companies, and those bills exist at the present time. Therefore they are not interested in a proposal that would put them further into debt. What they want is a chance to sell some of their wheat today in order to pay off those debts. They are not interested in going further into debt, especially at an interest rate of 5 per cent.
These meetings gave very careful consideration to the proposal of the western wheat conference and the resolution that was submitted to the government by the wheat conference and by the western provinces. It was a proposal that the government should advance to the farmers up to 50 per cent of the normal wheat delivery. There was strong support for the principle of that proposal.
The only thing the meeting did not like was the rather vague definition of "normal delivery expected". They said that might mean 8, 6, or perhaps only 4 bushels. So they suggested that, instead of using that form, they should say "up to 50 per cent of at least 8 bushels per cultivated acre." That is the basis upon which delivery was made last year and judging from what the minister said we have reason to hope that there will be a similar delivery this year.

The fact that we may have a similar delivery this year does not help the situation today. Today the farmers are in the very difficult position of having debts piled up. Every time they go to town they have to meet their creditors. Though they have wheat on the farms by means of which they should be able to liquidate those debts, they are not able to sell it. They also stress the fact that the government is largely in control of the wheat market. It took only 8 bushels in 195455, but there is no chance for farmers to deliver even a one-bushel quota at many points today. Therefore they feel the government should be prepared to make advances up to 50 per cent of at least 8 bushels per acre.
The minister argued that the only safe way to make loans would be through the banks, and that there would be little security by any other means. I am not going to debate that point, because the farmers are not asking for loans. They are asking for advances. The minister keeps making the alternative between bank loans and loans through the wheat board, but that is not what the farmers are asking for. They are asking that advances be made, and they would be quite prepared to give title to the wheat on their farms in return for these advances. Therefore the question of security does not arise. That is actually what is done in the United States under the sealed storage program.
Before I begin on another phase, may I call it one o'clock?

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made it quite plain that he believes it is to the advantage of Canada to maintain a surplus of wheat. He has also emphasized the fact that he believes the government should be prepared to relieve the farmers of some of the burden created by storage charges on the wheat held by the elevators, but on the other hand he does not feel that the surplus position creates any burden upon the farmer.
I would agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce wholeheartedly that it is in the national interest to maintain a substantial reserve of wheat. We feel that a reserve of wheat should be maintained as a national responsibility so that in the event of a series of crop failures we would have enough wheat on hand to meet domestic requirements as

well as to fill the demand from foreign markets. But we do not believe that the farmers should be required to finance the cost of maintaining that reserve.
I should like to quote what the minister said on this point, as found at page 129 of Hansard of January 16:
As far as the long-term situation is concerned, it seemed to me it was a hardship on the western farmer that he should be required to pay the carrying charges at the level required when grain storage is filled for practically twelve months in the year.
This is the point I want to draw to the attention of the house.
Apart from that, it did not seem to me that there was any particular burden on the farmer through this condition of plenty.
Toward the bottom of the same page he said:
We shall endeavour to see that hardship is not permitted to fall on the producer, but we are glad to have surpluses, particularly at a time when, in so many areas, we have acute shortages that hold within themselves the seeds of inflation.
As I say, we agree wholeheartedly with the minister on the desirability of maintaining a substantial reserve, but we do not agree with the minister that by merely paying the storage charges on a certain portion of the wheat held in storage in the elevators the burden is being lifted from the farmers. The minister apparently feels that it does not cost any more to produce and harvest a big crop than it does a medium one.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have never said that and I do not agree with the suggestion. I do know that the size of the crop makes a difference.

If the minister does not agree with that, I cannot understand why he should suggest that there is no burden on the farmers in carrying surpluses, because when they have been able to sell only a certain amount of wheat under a quota, the amount they have sold is only equivalent to quite a small crop.

The average in Alberta for the last year or two has been around 27 bushels, and the average in the area that I represent runs around 25. Right now in the good crop gumbo areas it runs around 35.

average yield now is probably around 35, but over a long period I should imagine that on the gumbo plains it would be about 25.
We are faced with this situation. When a large crop is in sight the farmer has to consider whether he can harvest that crop with his existing machinery. In some cases he may feel he will have to buy additional machinery. In some cases he may feel that his machinery is worn out and that new machinery should be bought. On the other hand, if he decides to try to harvest a heavy crop with machinery that he knows is in poor condition he is very liable to be faced with heavy costs resulting from breakdowns and loss of time, and heavy costs resulting from repair bills. He will have additional costs for fuel and labour and the additional cost of providing storage for that heavy crop. Therefore until the surplus wheat now on the farms is sold, the farmers are faced with the debts which were accumulated as a result of raising that heavy crop.
Of course it is not only the farmer who is suffering in the rural areas. Another person who is suffering just as much as the farmer, and in some cases even more, is the small, local businessman who in many cases has acted as the farmer's banker, advanced him credit and allowed him to obtain supplies without even signing a note. Many of these small businessmen have their backs to the wall today. They are in a position where the wholesalers will not allow them to have any more goods unless they pay cash. If any goods are shipped to them they are shipped c.o.d., and they cannot even lift them from the station without paying for them. I know many good businessmen, though perhaps they have been a little bit too generous, who are having a lot of difficulty in carrying on at the present time.
I find that in most cases the old established farmer is able to meet these costs from his savings. He is in that fortunate position. Many of the older farmers who are hoping to retire shortly are having to use a lot of the money upon which they intended to retire to meet current costs of operation which cannot be met by the sale of wheat. The minister will undoubtedly argue that this situation will soon be remedied, and that as soon as they can sell their wheat they can replace their savings. That is true, but unfortunately many farmers are not in that fortunate position. I have in mind particularly the younger farmers, and it is these new farmers who are really caught in the squeeze today.
Take the position of the young farmer buying a farm on time. Many of the older farmers who started farming in the west between 1910 and 1920 are now retiring, and

In closing I will say this. In view of the fact that there are some farmers who will be obliged to seek help under this legislation, we intend to support it. Nevertheless we feel that it falls far short of meeting the needs of this situation.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment briefly on this specific resolution. As I understand it, the main purpose of the legislation is to ease the critical cash shortage among prairie farmers. As a westerner I certainly sympathize with that objective.
As hon. members know, out in western Canada our wheat surplus recently reached the almost fantastic figure of one billion bushels. Our farmers are literally buried in wheat. Unfortunately, however, deliveries are so small that the farmers can get hardly enough cash to pay current living expenses. There is a very real cash shortage. That shortage is being reflected in reduced retail sales; and through lower retail sales I think harm is being done to the manufacturing industries of the east, such as the farm implement industry, the automobile industry and

so on. I therefore suggest that today there is real reason for parliament to consider giving the western farmer a helping hand.
This afternoon I have no particular political axe to grind, but I must say that I agree with those who have already participated in this debate and said that this resolution is unsatisfactory and inadequate. I am convinced that the desired objective, namely that of helping to ease the cash shortage in the west, could be achieved more effectively by cash advances on farm-stored grain. What is more, Mr. Chairman, if the truth were known I think many Liberal members from the prairies and even one or two cabinet ministers may think likewise.
What is the weakness of the proposal we are now discussing? I think the main weakness is simply that there will not be many farmers who will use it. Today most farmers who live on the prairies can borrow money from the banks on the security of wheat, without this legislation. I admit that there will be the odd one whose credit is perhaps not too good, who will need it. But by and large that is not the case. The majority of our western farmers today are reluctant to go further into debt to the banks than they are at the present time. That is why I say I do not think they will use this legislation.
We had the same kind of act on the statute books back in 1951. It was virtually useless then. I think it is going to be virtually useless today. As a matter of fact I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce must agree with that statement because out in Calgary, I think it was on November 28, he made this statement:
It is my hope and belief that comparatively limited use will be made of the lending facilities.
As I see it, all this legislation is going to do in the west is create more dissatisfaction, more resentment and more discontent. Almost without exception I think it is fair to say that our farm leaders, co-operatives, farm unions, wheat pools and the like have asked for cash advances on farm-stored grain.
The mechanics of such a scheme would be simple. Elevator agents would make cash advances against the quota book, on a basis decided by this parliament. Perhaps the advance would be 50 cents a bushel; maybe it would be 60 cents a bushel. That would be a matter for hon. members to decide.
The advantages to the farmer of such a scheme are obvious. In the first place there are many more elevators than there are banks, and it would be much more convenient for him to go to those agents. In the second place, I think the interest rate would be lower if the matter were handled through the board.

Despite what the minister said this morning, I am convinced that the Canadian wheat board could borrow money at a lesser rate than 5 per cent. The collection of the advance would be automatic, because the amount of the advance would be repaid as the grain was delivered. Above all, as far as the farmer is concerned, when he obtained an advance he would be getting his own money. He would be getting money that he would not have to worry about paying back. It would not be money that was simply another loan.
Why has the government rejected cash advances? It cannot be because of cost to the taxpayer. In asking for cash advances the western farmer is not just asking for another government subsidy. The amount of the advance would be deducted from his payment when he delivered his grain. The interest could be deducted from his last participation certificate when the final settlement was made. I do not think cash advances would need to cost the taxpayer a single, solitary cent.
Why does the Minister of Trade and Commerce appear to oppose cash advances? In his speech last week he suggested that those who are asking for cash advances are out to destroy the Canadian wheat board. I do not think the minister would expect that statement to be taken seriously by this house or by people in the west. He knows, as well as do most hon. members, that the very people who have been asking for cash advances, such as the farm unions, co-operatives, wheat pools and the like, are those who support the wheat board most vigorously. If they thought this action would in any way endanger the Canadian wheat board, I do not think they would be making the request for cash advances.
In the second place the minister intimated that this program of cash advances would be beyond the capacity of the wheat board to administer. I find it rather difficult to accept such reasoning also. To say that the wheat board is not able to handle cash advances is a reflection on the ability and competence of the staff of the board. I do not think such an intimation has much justification.
As we deal with this problem, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that we should bear in mind the fact that neither guaranteed bank loans nor cash advances are going to do much to solve the over-all wheat surplus problem. Neither proposal will sell one extra bushel of wheat. But in my judgment cash advances would be infinitely more effective as an emergency measure than the legislation now before us, for getting cash into the hands of the

Grain
farmers. I shall, if a vote comes, reluctantly support the resolution which is now before us.

When the s-peech from the
throne was being discussed, I did not participate in the debate though there was a great deal of interest amongst members in that particular debate. I knew that all these measures of particular importance to us would reappear later in the form of resolutions and bills and that I would have an opportunity of expressing my views on them. This is the first such resolution, and probably the most contentious of the lot, that is before us for discussion today.
The resolution refers to a situation which developed last fall in western Canada. As the house is fully aware, a shortage of cash developed as the result of inability to deliver grain to the elevators, particularly at harvest time. Of course this created a serious problem. There were meetings and discussions all over the three western provinces in an attempt to solve the problem. The idea of cash advances appeared to be the easiest solution, and certainly was the one that had the most appeal throughout the three western provinces. As a matter of fact it spread over the west like a prairie fire. Of course our friends in the opposition from Saskatchewan, Manitoba, the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Prince Albert were right there to fan the fire.
However, I think we can all agree that producers and everybody have a great deal of regard for cash advances as such. I believe we can say that everybody agrees with cash advances, but when you try to translate the idea of those cash advances into a practical scheme that would be acceptable to everybody then indeed there are many opinions. Many and varied schemes evolved out of the discussion. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, no matter what you term it, if you make an advance on a certain commodity, in this case wheat, it is still a loan. Inevitably there will be interest charges and administrative costs. There will be losses in any scheme of this nature.
If the person who receives the loan or the advance is unable, for one reason or another, to deliver the grain he still has an obligation to make good with money. In effect, a cash advance is just another term for a loan. At this point I should like to refer to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris who, in his speech early in the debate, made the ridiculous and I think childish assertion that the government were accusing the western farmer of dishonesty because they required guarantees in making loans.
