I believe this suggestion was also taken up today by the hon. member for Assiniboia. Of course we all know that any institution that lends money,

particularly other people's money, has an obligation to ensure that this money is repaid. They must get a guarantee in one form or another. I feel it is ridiculous to suggest that just because we are asking for a guarantee we are questioning the honesty of the farmers.
After all, even if a man cannot meet his financial obligations on a certain day it is certainly no indication that he is dishonest. It does happen, as we all know, that farmers, like everybody else, miscalculate and things do not work out exactly as planned. I believe the farmers themselves, as well as the farm organizations, would insist that an organization such as the wheat board operate in an efficient manner. I can understand our socialist friends being very free with other people's money, but I am a little surprised at hearing the suggestion from the hon. member, for Brandon-Souris, who is conservative in more than one sense.
Then we come to the hon. member for Prince Albert, to whom I referred previously. In the discussions in this house and outside, more recently outside, he has tried to make much of the statement the Minister of Trade and Commerce made in the course of an earlier speech. The hon. member tried to ridicule the suggestion by the minister that the members of the board would have presented their resignations if they had been called upon to administer such a scheme. The inference was that the minister was being run by the board. I think the people of Canada know the Minister of Trade and Commerce well enough to know that if he were convinced a measure was sound he would have found ways of implementing it.
It may be true that the hon. member for Prince Albert, or even the opposition, is not interested in knowing the feeling of the members of the Canadian wheat board but I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that every producer was very much interested in finding out exactly how the members of the wheat board felt about this question. I am sure the producers gave full weight to the advice of the board on such an important question. After all, the board would be charged with the responsibility of administering the scheme, and if they have such strong feelings on the matter there must be sound reasons for it. When statements like that are made throughout the country, invariably the impression is created that the members of the Canadian wheat board have other interests at heart than the primary interest of the Canadian producer. There is no other way the suggestion can be interpreted.
I believe either we have trust and faith in the members of the board or we have

Grain
not. But it does not mean we have to blindly follow their advice. When they take such a strong view, you cannot just dismiss it. According to the hon. member for Prince Albert, he would fire the whole board overnight without batting an eye. Apparently that is what the producers could expect from the Conservative party if they were responsible for administering the board.
While I am on this subject, may I protest against the charges that are repeatedly made, and were made recently in this house, against a civil servant who in my opinion is doing his best for the producer in spite of the very great difficulties. I refer to our transport controller. Surely even if you do not agree with his results or methods you will at least give him credit for discharging his duties honestly and looking after the interests of the producer. I know for a fact that is how he discharges his duties and I know that he is very conscientious and anyone who suggests that as controller of the board he is catering to interests other than those of the producer is being extremely unfair to this man. That charge has been reiterated again and again in this house. I feel it is unfair for the controller-
Where are the box cars?
As I said before, Mr. Chairman, even if you are the controller you do not manufacture box cars-
But you are supposed to control them.
-and the hon. member for Assiniboia should know that as well as anyone else.
He lost them in the United States.

If he cannot, is that an indication that his integrity should be challenged? It is perhaps a matter of opinion as to whether or not his efficiency can be challenged but surely it does not give us the right to challenge his integrity, and that is an entirely different matter.
I see that you agree he is no good; that is fair enough.

The point I am making at this time is that we have no right to challenge his integrity. I can assure the hon. member that we will discuss the other point relating to the transport controller at another time in this house; I shall be very glad to discuss it with him in this house.
A statement has been made by another hon. member from the west to which I should like to refer briefly. I refer to a statement
made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Trainor). I am sorry to observe that he is not in his seat; possibly I should have sent him a note but I assumed that he would be here when I spoke. However, the hon. member took it upon himself to moralize earlier in this house on this question. I must confess I believe he got a bit mixed up in his morals. Nevertheless, he in turn issued a challenge to hon. members to appear on a platform in a farming community. I observe that the hon. member is coming into the chamber now and I want at this time to give him a little kindly advice. I think he should revise his thinking in relation to the wheat board before appearing on a platform before an audience of farmers or grain producers. In the course of his remarks he referred to the wheat board's operation and termed it the charity of the Canadian taxpayer. There is nothing the farmers resent more than to have the operation of the board referred to as operating on the public charity because, as we all know and as has been explained time and time again-although apparently it has not penetrated my hon. friend's mind as yet -the board is an entirely separate operation from the government. It does not operate with public money but borrows money for the operation of the board and operates for the benefit of the producer and finally redistributes the money back to the producer. There is nothing which farmers generally resent more than to be told that the board operates as a charity from the Canadian taxpayers. I think it would be nice if the hon. member could bear that in mind before leaving the chamber.
There is, however, another misconception in the hon. member's mind which I do not intend to deal with at too great length because it is an involved question and I observed that it reappeared in the speech given by the Leader of the Opposition earlier this morning. I am referring to the nonsensical view that the government buys wheat from the farmers and that the whole procedure operates out of public money, confusing the two and trying to lay the blame there.
This point was taken up by the Leader of the Opposition this morning and was used as the basis of his argument. This is an old argument which we have heard for years, ever since the inception of the wheat board. The most staunch opponent of the Canadian v/heat board has used this argument in and out of the house incessantly since the inception of the board. The Leader of the Opposition laboured the point this morning that the government was "forcing" the farmer. Let me say if there has ever been a case of voluntary

Grain
compulsion the wheat board is a good example. The Leader of the Opposition said in effect that the farmer has been forced into an impossible position. That is the effect of the argument advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg South which was taken again by the Leader of the Opposition. I can assure both the hon. members that the farmers of western Canada and certainly all of the farm organizations can see through that argument and they have long since seen through it. As a matter of fact, it is the very argument which is causing the farmers great concern, in asking the government to share the cost of operation of any cash advance. Early last month in Winnipeg a western conference was held attended by nine farm organizations and others who met to discuss the question of cash advances. I think the discussion was more on a scheme of a permanent nature and most of the discussion was along that line, but it was based on the assumption that the government would take the responsibility for the interest and administration of the scheme. When the argument to which I have just referred was brought forward the delegates at the convention took a second look at it before asking the government to implement such a scheme, and the resolution instead of being passed was referred back to a special committee for further consideration before being presented. I am simply saying this in passing to indicate that this is an old argument and that the farm organizations in particular can see through it.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre took the position this afternoon, if I understood him correctly, that the farmers and the farm organizations were unanimous in asking for cash advances through the wheat board as the responsibility of the wheat board. I submit that this is not what the Leader of the Opposition on the one hand and the Conservative party on the other have been advocating. I followed the speech of the Leader of the Opposition very closely this morning in an endeavour to ascertain what his position was in relation to this matter and I must admit that I am still not too clear on the subject. He referred to the loans being made through the ordinary channel of the wheat board as an ordinary payment. That would be exactly what the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre advocated. However, in his concluding remarks the Leader of the Opposition added that the government should pay the interest. Did he mean that the government should pay the administrative costs and the losses? No one speaks of losses, although there are bound to be some losses,

and it remains to be seen exactly what his position is on that point because it makes all the difference in the world.
I agree that in all likelihood the farm organizations will support-not without reluctance, concern and perhaps with some modifications-a scheme of cash advances if the government assumes all the responsibility. However, when you examine the basis on which it has been put by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, that the board should take full responsibility, I doubt at this moment if you could get any farm organization to endorse the proposition. Certainly it is the scheme advocated by the farmers' union because in their resolution they ask the government to assume the administrative and interest charges and I have yet to see a farm organization which has come out clearly for a cash advance through the ordinary channel of the wheat board with the board assuming all responsibility. This is the very scheme to which the wheat board itself took very great exception.
I am convinced that any fair-minded man will realize there are grave dangers in such a proposition. Of course, it depends-
What is the difference between the wheat board and the government?
Do you not know the difference?

I am glad that the hon. member for Winnipeg South has placed that remark on the record and I shall repeat it to make sure that it is on the record. The hon. member has asked what the difference is between the wheat board and the government. 1 would suggest that he attend several farmers' meetings and become informed on the subject, because I do not intend to take the few minutes at my disposal to explain it to him.
As I said, Mr. Chairman, the crux of the whole problem is:	who will assume the
responsibility in connection with any such loans and losses incurred through their operation? I would think that, at least in our part of the country and I believe generally, a great many producers would raise serious objections. You run into a great many difficulties. The farmers who do not ask for loans would have to help pay for the cost of the loans made to others. In all the discussion that has taken place since last fall on that particular point there has been no unanimity. I repeat that I doubt very much if you could get any farm organization to pass such a resolution.
When you ask the government to assume all the cost then you remove one of the main difficulties in connection with cash advances. But if we are to do that let us be fair and

admit it is an entirely different proposition when you ask the treasury to provide outright assistance. Speaking for myself and my district and Manitoba as a whole, I think the first question that would be asked, even by the farm organizations, would be, "What about the farmer who has had no crop?" There are many parts where they have had no crops for a few years, and certainly where they had no crop last year. Would they not expect to receive assistance on the same basis as those who have had a big crop? That raises another serious question to be resolved.
I am just mentioning these things in passing to indicate that the problem is by no means as simple as the opposition would like us to believe. When you talk of cash advances in general there is no difficulty, but before they can be put into operation the government must translate them into one specific scheme or another. Let us remember that when the emergency occurred three months ago a solution had to be found or a temporary expedient adopted in as short a time as possible.
At the present time throughout the western provinces the emphasis is being placed on a permanent scheme, call it cash advances or loans, in connection with farm-stored grain. I submit that this is another proposition entirely. This is a loan with the grain as security. Reference has been made to the United States scheme, but that is an entirely different proposition. This is not something new as it has been debated fully on at least two occasions in the past year. There are advantages and there are disadvantages.
So far the farm organizations throughout the country have not yet found a solution or a scheme that would be generally acceptable. It depends a great deal on how it is operated and on world conditions. If there were a need for it, that would be a good reason to institute such a system; but, as I say, it is a different system.
That is why, at the western conference held in Winnipeg last December, after due consideration they referred it back to a committee for further study. There may be merit in it, but the point is that cash advances in general do not mean very much. There must be something specific. There is no point in saying that farmers as a whole or farm organizations will support the idea of the wheat board being fully responsible for all administrative costs and so on that would be entailed. It all depends on how it is worked out.
As I say, this occurred three months ago and these bank loans were not popular and are not popular. But they have helped some people, particularly smaller operators, to a degree. The only real solution is to get the grain moving. We are fortunate that the grain
Grain
is moving at the moment. I do not want to anticipate the other debate, as two of the previous speakers have, but I think it can be shown clearly that the policy pursued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in connection with grain has been fully vindicated and will be fully vindicated in the months to come.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a minute to comment on one or two statements made by the hon. member for Provencher, who has just resumed his seat. It seems to me that the hon. member devoted all of his speech to an attempt to becloud the issue. In other words he was following the technique of setting up a straw man, setting up something that nobody has really asked for, and then proceeding to knock it down.
One statement in particular to which I take objection is the statement by the hon. member for Provencher that the Conservatives would fire all the members of the wheat board. No one has ever said any such thing. One or two people in our party have said, and I think all of us would be prepared to say the same, that they doubted very much the minister's statement that the members of the wheat board would all resign if cash advances were brought in. That is a very different thing entirely.
I am not going to bother going into the other matters which the hon. member for Provencher mentioned, because I think in the course of my remarks I will be replying to him in more detail.
The measure before the house was brought forward to validate action already taken by the government in an effort to relieve the shortage of cash in the hands of the farmers due to their inability to market grain over the past several months. Everyone in western Canada realizes the seriousness of that situation of shortage of cash. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has attempted throughout to minimize the seriousness of the situation and as has been indicated by several speakers-I will not repeat this-it seems quite evident that he expects that very little use will be made of this measure, that not many farmers will take advantage of it. I think the measure is being brought in deliberately to ensure that as few farmers as possible will take advantage of it, only those who are absolutely desperate; and of those, only the ones whom the bank considers good risks will get any benefit from it.
I think there are two considerations which we should keep particularly in mind as far as this legislation is concerned. The first is the adequacy of the measure to meet

Grain
the situation which prevails and the second is whether there is an alternative measure which could be put into force to meet the situation more satisfactorily in place of the measure put forward by the government. I think on both counts there is no question that this is a pitifully inadequate piece of legislation for the situation it is designed to meet. I will be going into that in more detail.
This morning the minister said that this legislation was required solely-he stressed the word "solely"-because of the large crops of the past five years, and later on in his speech he said it was due to an abundant rainfall, that that was the only reason the legislation was necessary. Apparently in his thinking the minister leaves out of consideration altogether the effect of a large surplus of wheat in the United States and the fact that that is being disposed of-he has complained of this frequently-under give-away plans and things of that sort. He leaves out of consideration entirely the fact that there is a great deal more wheat being grown in Europe and in other parts of the world. In other words, apparently he fails completely to recognize that this is anything but a temporary situation which one or two poor crops will correct. It would appear at the present time that it is not a temporary situation. We must all admit that this particular measure is purely a temporary solution, one that will have no long-range effects whatever, and that we should not be thinking in these terms at all. What we should really be considering here is some means to meet what looks as though it would be a serious long-term situation as regards the disposal of the western wheat crop.
The minister went on to say in his usual optimistic manner that sales will be made in sufficient quantities so that farmers will be able to deliver approximately the same amount of wheat as was the case from the
1953-54 crop. What did they deliver from that crop? Under the stress of circumstances they delivered an eight-bushel per acre quota. In some cases they were not able to deliver the eight bushels per cultivated acre. If a farmer had a half-section farm with 300 acres under cultivation, he would be able to deliver 2,400 bushels of grain, which would net him, considering grades and so forth, not a great deal more than $2,400-maybe $200 or $300 more than that at the most-in most parts of western Canada. Considering his expenses, that is not sufficient to enable him to carry on operations, to meet the living expenses of himself and his family, to feed and clothe them and so forth, to pay his taxes and continue in business. Even if we are able to

take from the farmers as much grain as was taken from them in the previous year, they are still going to be in a very serious situation in most cases.
The minister then went on to say that cash advances meant putting the wheat board into the lending business, and the member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras) repeated that in the usual parrot-like fashion that the members of the Liberal party follow as far as the pronouncements of the Minister of Trade and Commerce are concerned. It has been pointed out by several other people, and I pointed it out myself only a few days ago, in the throne speech debate, that cash advances being made through the agency of the wheat board do not turn the wheat board into a loaning institution. A very great distinction must be made here between a loan made by a chartered bank or any other loaning institution, on the basis of a lien against wheat held by a farmer, and an advance made by one of the agents of the wheat board to a farmer for grain he has on his farm and is ready to deliver to the wheat board. As a matter of fact, the agents of the wheat board would be doing exactly the same thing as they are doing all the time and have been doing for many years past.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
May I ask the
hon. member a question? Would there not be a difference? In the first case the bank has security for the advance and in the second case there is no security in the hand.
Yes, I think that the wheat board has more complete security than any bank would have, for this reason, that no farmer can deliver any grain and sell any grain except through the wheat board.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is not true.

The minister says it is not true. The only other place he can sell any grain is to a neighbour or to another farmer. Of course, that brings up another point. There is a great deal of what, strictly speaking, under the Wheat Board Act, is illegal trade going on, that is what the minister is referring to. In other words, what has happened as a result of the extremely tight cash situation is the development of a black market or a free market, or whatever you want to call it, underneath the regular wheat board market for grain. Farmers are selling grain in that market at prices as much as 50 per cent below the regular prices quoted by the wheat board, and in many cases even less than 50 per cent. That is what the minister is referring to. But, as far as the ordinary legal sale of grain is concerned, and except for a very limited quantity which can be disposed of to farmers

in the feeding business, the only market a farmer has is the wheat board. I do not think the minister will dispute that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I know of considerable quantities-and so does my hon. friend-being sold to feeders, and that is quite a legitimate transaction, as far as I know.
I have just said that there is a certain amount being sold, and most of it is being sold at very low prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If advances had been made on that wheat by the wheat board, what would have happened then?

If advances had been made on that by the wheat board, the farmer would not be in the position of having to sell it at these ridiculously low prices. He would have the money in his pocket. He would get twice the price he is getting at the present time. The only reason why anybody is selling grain at 60 cents and 70 cents a bushel, when the quoted price of the wheat board for it is $1.70 for No. 1 at Fort William, is that he is desperately in need of cash. As somebody remarked to me not very long ago, you cannot starve a farmer. You can introduce all kinds of regulations that might conceivably have that effect, but he will beat them. He will not starve. He will find some means of living.
He can live on wheat.

Nobody wants to live on a pure diet of wheat, but farmers are finding a means of getting cash in spite of the situation they are in and they will probably continue to do so. However, that is getting away from the main point I was following, which is that the elevator agents of the wheat board have been taking in grain from the farmers, making out cheques to them to cover the initial payment, and to have them make out similar cheques to cover grain on the farm-grain that they know is on the farm-is essentially the same thing. It does not involve any new administrative machinery. It does not involve anything that is going to cost a great deal of money. It can be done extremely simply and without any real risk because the farmer who has had a cash advance, unless he dies or goes out of the farming business, cannot deliver any grain without repaying that cash advance. In other words, he is in a strait-jacket as far as trying to get out of repaying that cash advance is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not like to keep interrupting, but reference is made to the farmer who has liens on his grain. The
Grain
liens would take precedence over those cash advances, I suppose, would they not?
As a matter of fact, I do not think they would.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, they would. I assure you they would.
The municipal lien does.

The municipal lien does, but the other liens do not. As a matter of fact, what does the farmer want the money for except to pay off these liens, these taxes and so forth? That is why he is trying to get the cash advances. The various points the minister is trying to make are further efforts to becloud the real issue. In that connection the minister said this morning that the farmer would be shopping around and trying to get someone to give him cash advances. That statement is ridiculous.
That is not what he said at all.
That is exactly what he said.
It is not.

He said it would be an undesirable thing. As a matter of fact, every farmer deals with one or two elevator men at the most and in most cases he leaves his permit book with the elevator agent. It stays there right at the elevator. He brings in grain when he is able to deliver it and it is marked off against his permit book. If the amount of the cash advance were entered in the permit book there would be no difficulty in collecting the money save in very exceptional circumstances. I admit there is no operation of any kind in which there is not some slight risk, but I would submit that the amount of loss which would occur under a scheme of that sort would be infinitesimal.
The minister also tried to maintain this morning that cash advances would not be cheaper as far as the farmers are concerned. He went on to say that the board borrows money at 3 per cent but that if the board were making cash advances the administrative costs would be at least 2 per cent more. I do not know on what basis he says they would be 2 per cent more. As I have just indicated, I cannot see where the administrative costs would amount to anything. The elevator agents, who are acting as agents of the board, are there carrying on their operations and as part of their ordinary activities and without any more remuneration, because they would be issuing cheques anyway, they could make these cash advances. In other words, there is no need to have a big administrative set-up in order to administer such a scheme, and rather than

Grain
the cost of it being 2 per cent I would think it would much more likely be one-tenth of 1 per cent or perhaps less than that.
There was one point touched on by the hon. member for Provencher which was not touched on by the minister. In none of his statements does the minister seem to acknowledge the responsibility of the board and the government, because the board is an agency of the government. There has been no admission of the responsibility of the board and the government to take this wheat off the farmers' hands because of the fact that the wheat board is the only market the farmer has. When you put into operation a legal monopoly system of any kind-there are plenty of legal monopolies, as the Minister of Justice knows-then whatever the purpose of the monopoly there are certain responsibilities that go with the granting of the monopoly. The person or persons having the monopoly are required to give certain services.
Take the case of a railway serving a certain area. They have a monopoly on that form of business in that area, and whether or not it is profitable for them to do so they are required to run trains on that line. There are many branch lines throughout the country on which the railways lose a lot of money but they are still required to run trains on those lines. When they apply for the discontinuance of service on such branch lines in most cases they are turned down. As I say, any monopoly position carries the responsibility of giving service. The government and the wheat board, having a monopoly on the marketing of grain, consequently have the responsibility of taking the grain off the farmers' hands. The farmers have no place else to sell it, and if the government and the board do not take it off their hands they should at least put cash in the farmers' hands in the form of cash advances so that they will be able to finance their operations, eat, clothe themselves and their families and carry on in a normal manner.
I do not think the government can escape from that position. They have a monopoly position in the marketing of grain through their agency, the wheat board, and therefore they have the responsibility of handling the grain. The minister also went on, as several other speakers have indicated, to give us a little lecture and say that we must be careful what we say in criticism of the government and our general wheat position because there is great danger that what we say here may have the result of causing people to refuse to buy our grain, of knocking down the price and so on. I would say the minister cannot have it both ways. Quite frequently

he tells members of the opposition in the house that it does not matter what we say anyway, that we are not going to have any influence and are not going to change matters by a lot of talk. However, that having been his position with respect to a considerable number of matters, I do not think he can now turn around and say: "You must not say a word about wheat because you may ruin a sale or two." In addition, it is a ridiculous position for the minister to take because he knows just as well as I do that the people acting as buyers for other countries know the general wheat and grain situation in the world just as well as we do. Nothing we say here is going to give away any secrets or make any difference in the attitude of people buying grain.
The minister made another statement which I thought was very questionable. He said that the board has not reduced prices and it is still selling wheat. As a matter of fact, the board has reduced prices considerably on the lower grades of wheat. They had large amounts of No. 5, No. 6 and feed wheat which were not selling. As far back as three or four years ago they were urged to reduce the price to some extent so as to place this wheat in a competitive position with barley and oats as a feed grain and they refused to do so. But finally in the last year they did reduce the prices of these low grades of wheat and as a result considerable amounts have been sold. In other words, this is an indication of the fact that, in spite of what the minister says, low grade wheat in any event is still susceptible to the law of supply and demand and that if you reduce prices you can make sales.
That, as I say, has been done, and I am glad it has been done. This move has not yet succeeded in getting a good deal of this low grade grain out of the elevators and thus making room for the better grade crop we grew last year.
It took them a long time to do it.

As the hon. member for Winnipeg South says, it took them a long time to take this really sensible step and start to get rid of the low grade grain which was clogging the entire marketing set-up.
To sum up the situation briefly, as I see it the loan scheme is completely inadequate to meet the existing situation. The government has admitted its inadequacy by bringing forward another resolution which will be considered shortly, to pay part of the storage costs on grain. In other words, what they have done is to make two stabs at the problem, both very ineffective, instead of looking

at the situation, realizing how serious it was and taking some really useful step in order to solve it.
The next point is that the maximum amount of $1,500 by way of a loan is too small. It is not sufficient to meet the farmer's harvesting expenses and carry him through the winter. Let us take as an example the half-section farmer, not the big farmer but the half-section farmer who had 200 acres in crop last year. It was a good year and we will say he got 30 bushels to the acre. He has 6,000 bushels of grain. In most cases the half-section farmer cannot afford to have his own combine because his operation is not big enough. Quite a number of such people have combines but they do custom work for other people. We will take the more ordinary case where the man does not own a combine. He has to have his grain custom-combined. In my part of the country at any rate it would cost $5 an acre to have the grain swathed and combined. In other words, the half-section farmer had an expenditure of $1,000 simply to have his grain cut and put in his granaries, which would leave him if he got the maximum loan-he probably would not get the maximum with a half-section farm-with $500 for all the rest of his expenses, $500 on which he and his family have to live and with which to put in a crop next spring. The thing is ridiculous. It just does not meet the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is ridiculous to say the loan was intended to carry a farmer for a year.
I am not saying it was intended to carry him for a year, but certainly it must have been intended to carry him through the winter-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

-and to let him eat during that period and get enough money or enough credit to buy oil and so forth to put in his crop next spring. In other words, surely it must be designed to carry him six months because he is not going to get any other income before that time.
Wheat is not the only thing he grows.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: He is selling wheat every month.

In a number of cases it is the only thing. If it were not for the fact that the majority of farmers have some livestock the situation would really be disastrous. They would be in a starving situation at the present time. As the hon. member for Assini-boia has said, they would be reduced to eating nothing but their own wheat. Fortunately
Grain
the majority of them have some livestock. There are quite a few who are without any livestock and they are entirely dependent on grain which they produce. As I say, I think there is no question that the amount of the loan is completely inadequate. It is far too small and it will not serve the purpose for which it was intended.
Where do the farmers live who have no livestock?
There are many of them living not far from where the hon. member is situated, right around Maple Creek.
Without livestock?

Yes. The next point is the interest rate. I am not going to dwell on this matter. However, I do not think there is any doubt that interest rates are dependent on the risks involved. You have a government guaranteed loan to begin with. The chances of the wheat not being delivered to offset the loan are remote. If by any chance that happens the government is taking up the slack. In these circumstances a 5 per cent rate of interest is not justified.
The minister himself said that the wheat board borrows money at 3 per cent. In cases like this, if the matter is going to be handled in this way, the interest rate should be down to the same amount, in my opinion, namely 3 per cent. The other great difficulty is that many farmers have not been able to get this loan. That is the information I received. I should be interested in getting from the minister before this debate closes how many farmers have applied for a loan and how many have been given a loan; in other words, what percentage of farmers have been turned down as far as this loan is concerned? I think those figures would be extremely illuminating.
The complete inadequacy of this measure to meet the desperate shortage of cash which exists in western Canada has been quite adequately shown, in my opinion, by the speeches made on this side of the house so far today and during the speech from the throne. I would hope that the government would pay sufficient attention to those speeches to lead them to try to devise something better, or in other words, really to put into effect a system of cash advances such as that which has been urged on them by all the farm organizations in western Canada.

There are a few points with which I should like to deal in regard to this matter. The first point that I wish to make is in connection with the attempt to indicate that a cash advance on farm-stored grain, though it must be repaid, is not a loan. The fact that the opposition parties, by trying to

Grain
make out that advances against farm-stored grain which must be repaid are not a loan and are equivalent to selling the grain, indicates what a dangerous thing it is that they are advocating. The hon. member for Acadia indicated that in his area there were charges against the grain to the extent of in some cases perhaps 60 per cent of the value. If what is advocated by the opposition were done, and if advances were made against that farm-stored grain by the elevator company on behalf of the wheat board, what you would have would be this situation. When the time came to deliver the grain, the charges would have to be paid to the extent of 60 per cent and those loans would have to be paid to the extent of 50 per cent. There would not be enough to pay actually what was owing on the grain. Who would go short? Obviously the person who would go short would be the wheat board. As no statutory priority could be given to the wheat board, before any cheque could be issued to the wheat board all these prior liens would have to be met. So the farmer would be hauling wheat in to the elevator. He would get nothing for it for himself and there would not be enough to meet the wheat board requirements.
The hon. member for Acadia never said there were liens on it.
I want to develop this point.
Get it right.
Is this the eastern Tucker or the western Tucker?
I notice it is unpalatable for members of the opposition to look at the facts.
The hon. member for Acadia never said there were liens on it.
I heard what he said.
He never said there were liens on the grain and you know that could not have been possible.
I know what he said.
Are you speaking as the eastern Tucker or the western Tucker?

It is the same thing as a lien, if my hon. friend wants to make any distinction. Provincial law in this matter would apply as against the wheat board. It would not apply as against the bank. There is no use of members of the opposition trying to raise a whole lot of prejudice because the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that

if the matter were handled through the wheat board these prior liens and pledges would have priority over repayment to the wheat board, and that would mean that there would be severe losses. That statement was seized on in a characteristic way by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I refer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce saying that if the loans were made by the wheat board we could not give statutory priority to these advances or loans, and that there would be losses. That statement was distorted by the hon. member for Assiniboia to his saying that the Liberal party were accusing the farmers of being dishonest.
That is practically what the minister said.
Why do you not listen to what I am saying instead of being so anxious to say something different? Why do you not listen for a little while?
You are mixed up.
Two-tongued Tucker toeing the line.
The minister pointed out these facts which I think anybody who was ready to recognize the facts must recognize to be the truth.
He did not state the facts.

Then we are told by the hon. member for Assiniboia something that I was not surprised to hear. First of all, he laid down a false statement that the minister in effect accused the farmers of being dishonest. Then he went on to add, "We will certainly not let the people of Saskatchewan forget that statement".
Hear, hear.

My friend the hon. member for Dauphin says, "hear, hear". Those are the accepted tactics of the C.C.F. in western Canada.
As a matter of fact I think the people are getting dissatisfied with these tactics. First of all, there is a smear which has no basis in fact and then they say, "Now just watch out how we are going to make it stick to you". That is exactly what the hon. member for Assiniboia said this morning.
The tactics of Karl Marx.

As my hon. friend has just said, they are the accepted tactics of Karl Marx and I am not surprised at the members of the C.C.F. party following them.

Here is another example hinted at by an interruption. My hon. friends are glad to find that there is a Liberal newspaper which has put something on their editorial page about which they are already licking their lips in anticipation of how they are going to spread it all over Saskatchewan with regard to myself. Whether it is well founded or not does not worry the members of the C.C.F. party. Of course consistent with the attitude of Karl Marx which is, arouse hatred; that is the way to get into office. It does not much matter whether it is the right thing to arouse hatred as long as you get into office.
My hon. friends across the way have repeatedly taunted me with regard to the Free Press two-Tucker editorial. I shall therefore deal with it for a moment. Here is an extract from the editorial:
On the afternoon of October 17 the executive of the Liberal association met, 50 strong, in Rosthem. That evening the western Mr. Tucker wired Prime Minister St. Laurent and Trade Minister Howe and, on behalf of the meeting, pressed for cash advances on farm-stored grain.
But the air of Ottawa has caused a strange metamorphosis; . ...
True.
Read it all.

You can read it all if you want, but I believe it has already all been read in the house. I am pointing out that our executive asked for cash advances on farm stored grain. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, if that is not what this bill provides?
No.

Let us see what we are actually providing. The banks are authorized to make advances against the grain on the farm, on which there is given a statutory security. When that grain is delivered to the elevator, the agent to whom it is delivered must deduct half of the payment on the grain to repay that advance.
Seme hon. Members: No.

My hon. friends say no. I am stating exactly what I understand is provided. This is to be an advance against grain on the farm on which there is a statutory priority, and which is to be repaid out of the proceeds from that grain.
At 5 per cent.

We are not dealing with the interest rate at the moment, if my hon. friend will just keep his mind on one thing at a time. I am dealing with this question that it is alleged our executive asked for cash advances and when I said here in the house that what the government was proposing to
Grain
do was to make cash advances, then I am accused of taking a different stand from what my executive took. My point is that when you say the banks have a right to make an advance against grain on the farm, and if they make an advance they have security on the grain, and when the grain is delivered the debt must be repaid, then you are providing for cash advances against that grain.
You will never make that stick.
I may not be able to make it stick, but my hon. friend is rejoicing in the fact, whether or not it is true, that I will not be able to make it stick.
Are you differentiating between advances and loans?
Advances are exactly the same as loans.
The minister does not agree with that. He says everybody who asks for advances is a saboteur of the wheat board.
I am dealing with the question as I see it. The minister makes his own speeches. If my hon. friend thinks I have always got to agree with the minister, he is mistaken.
Hear, hear.
Start to show some of that disagreement.

My hon. friends opposite say I will not be able to make it stick. They do not want me to get the truth before this house for fear I might make it stick. So far as I am concerned, I was elected to this house 20 years ago. In the meantime, I have been elected twice to the legislature. My hon. friends may taunt me that I cannot make things stick, but my experience with the people of western Canada is this. If you are honest with them, they will give you their support. My hon. friends may laugh all they want, and they have tried very hard to beat me, but I still have faith that the people do support honesty in public life rather than dishonesty. If all my hon. friends can say when I am laying the facts before this house is that whether or not they are facts I cannot make them stick, then is not that coming down to a pretty low point in political life?
We say you cannot make them stick because they are not facts.

It is very interesting to me. I can listen to my hon. friends opposite without getting so uneasy that I have to keep yelling at them, because it is my attitude that

Grain
we are reasonable men and I can wait until I make my arguments and leave it to the good sense of the house. I am not afraid to have the opposition present their arguments, but it would look to me as if the opposition were afraid that some advantage they think they are going to be able to reap from this editorial may be taken away from them if I explain it. I wonder if that is their attitude? They jeer that I will not be able to make it stick, even although it is true.
I repeat that an advance against farm-stored grain, on which security is given and which must be repaid with interest, is a loan. Nobody can say anything different.
I do.
You can it if you want to, but you will be saying something that is incorrect and it would not be the first time.
We will let the farmers judge that.
There again we have the idea that you think you can make the farmers believe almost anything. 1 do not think you are going to make them believe that the Tory party-
You are judging me by yourself.

I do not think you are going to make the farmers believe the Tory party is more to be trusted to maintain the wheat board as the exclusive agency for the marketing of wheat than is the present government.
Talk about making things stick. You just try to make that stick out in western Canada. The people of western Canada remember how under a Tory government wheat on the open market was permitted to go down to a point where the farmers were getting 19 cents a bushel for No. 1 wheat. Those are the people who talk to us, those are the people-
Who established the wheat board?

Those are the people who say the wheat board should sell more wheat; that it should reduce the price. Yes, those are the people. They do not need to tell the farmers that is a Tory policy because the farmers know it.
Who established the wheat board?
If my hon. friend would just keep quiet I would not have referred to the unfortunate record of the Tory party in western Canada because it was not my intention to do so.
Is there a Tory party in western Canada?

Well, the remnants of it. As a matter of fact, I realize that all the time there is a definite attack upon the wheat board. They are attacked for not selling wheat fast enough. They say the board should reduce the price to get rid of it.
Now then, what would be the effect of that? We have had several years of good crops, but there will be periods again, and history shows it, when we will have short crops. What happened in the past before we had the wheat board was this. The farmer had to market his grain. It was sold on the open market and went into the hands of the speculators. The time came ultimately when the wheat was sold, and when it was sold in years of short crops the speculator got the better price. The farmer who had no wheat to sell did not benefit. It is for that reason I have believed in the wheat board for over 30 years. It is because year after year I saw periods of good crops in western Canada when the price would fall. Then, when we had short crops and the price went up, that did not benefit the farmer but it benefited those who bought the wheat. When there was any danger of oversupply such as there is today, they let the price go down to levels such as were experienced in 1932 when good No. 1 northern wheat was sold by the farmer for 19 cents a bushel.
Now then, so far as the Winnipeg Free Press is concerned, they are entitled to their opinion. They do not like the wheat board as a compulsory marketing agency for Canadian wheat.
I do not mind the Free Press disagreeing with me. In fact, Liberals disagree amongst themselves all the time, and that is the view of that newspaper. I hold a belief that the wheat board is a good thing for the western farmer, and a good thing for the Canadian economy. It is one of the things in which I believe with all my heart and soul. If it means my motives are to be questioned, if it means I may be driven out of public life,
I will stick to the thing in which I believe.
I do not care that much about my fate. Many of my hon. friends rejoice, thinking they have something there which indicates that I was dishonest and they hope to use it against me all over Saskatchewan and particularly in my own seat.
Oh, oh.

I know that the hon. member for Assiniboia would dearly love to use that against me but I want to say this: so far as I am concerned I have taken a stand which I think is right in this matter. I know they

Grain
will use that against me but it is not the first time I have been slandered by members of the C.C.F. party and I suppose it will not be the last. I do not propose to be deterred from saying what I think is in the best interests of the farmers of western Canada by any threats that have been made against me to the effect that I will be smeared up and that I will not be able to successfully answer their accusations.
It was not the C.C.F.
I say to every one of you, do the worst in your smear campaign; I rely on the good sense of my people.
Hear, hear.
Now, then, let me just deal with the facts of this matter-
Yes, let us get to the facts.
It's about time.
I was one of those who attended the marketing conference in Saskatoon from start to finish. I believe that the hon. member for Saskatoon was there for some of the time.
I was there all the time.
Well, I was one of those who attended all sessions and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle was another. I think the three of us were the only ones who were there at all times.
You are wrong again.

I think the hon. member for Prince Albert looked in two or three times.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the marketing conference was called by the interprovincial farm union council and they invited to that meeting the members of the farm unions, representatives of the pools and of the United Grain Growers, representatives of labour, chambers of commerce and so on.
I have in my hand a report of that meeting which was sent to me by the secretary of the meeting and so that there may be no doubt about it, I am going to read the first two resolutions passed at that conference. The first resolution that was laid down was to the effect that the wheat board had the confidence of the people present. The resolution was passed unanimously without a single dissenting voice and it read as follows:
That this conference express its confidence in the Canadian wheat board as a sound method of marketing Canadian grain.
That resolution was carried.
The next resolution concerned advances to farmers and reads as follows:
Motion as amended-
Observe that it was the motion as amended-
Be it resolved that the organizations participating in this conference urge the government of Canada to make immediate provision for advances to farmers on grain in store on the farm, and further that these advances should be up to one half the value of the normal delivery expected and should be repayable on the basis of one half of the value of each delivery made by the farmer.
This was the resolution finally passed by the conference but it was passed-as the hon. member for Saskatoon knows-only after a great deal of discussion and only after a resolution was brought forward representing what many of the farmers would like to have seen done; namely, have advances made through the wheat board. When this was brought forward, I think, by the representatives of the farm unions, it met with opposition. Various objections were raised by some of the people who were present, who said in effect that this procedure would involve the wheat board in the matter and put them in the position of trying to collect back money loaned from the farmers.

The
whole thing was a phony issue.

My hon. friend says it was a phony issue, but it was raised at that conference and in all sincerity. My hon. friend seems inclined to take the attitude that no one else but himself is sincere. I find that a most distasteful attitude. I think there were many people at that conference who were as sincerely concerned about the best interests of the farmer as my hon. friend from Moose Mountain. Of course, my hon. friend labours under the impression that only he and his group are honestly and sincerely concerned about the best interests of the farmer. I think that is a most despicable attitude. Among the people who took that attitude were leaders of the pool and they would not raise a phony issue.
Now let us talk about the pool annual convention.
I will come to that if you will just contain yourself in patience.
It will soon be time to quit.

I know that you are looking forward to the end of this discussion and I do not blame you. In any event the idea was brought forward that a very strong attack was being made upon the wheat board and that if something was laid upon it whereby it had to absorb losses and had to engage in

Grain
contests in the courts as to what should be done with the money from the wheat delivered to it and had to engage in collection of loans or advances it would involve the wheat board in something it was not set up to do. They said we would prefer that the wheat board be kept as a marketing agency and not be dragged into this field and they said further they did not want their elevator agents dragged into this field. They said they would not want the wheat board engaged in the business of trying to collect debts. This represented the attitude of some of the pool leaders. Finally it was decided to appoint a committee to draw up a resolution which would urge that the government provide for advances and leave it up to the government to decide how it should be done, after hearing any representations which might be made by organizations there represented. That was the considered opinion of this conference called by the farm unions and attended by representatives from all over western Canada including representatives of the provincial governments of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The provincial minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan supported this resolution.
That was a mistake, was it not?

Let my hon. friend tell the Hon. Mr. Nollet that.
I would like to refer again to the resolution that was passed. They wanted action from the government-
They sure did.

They decided it should be left to the government to decide what action should be taken to get money into the hands of the farmers and that it should be repaid. It surprises me to learn that some people think this was not asking for loans to be provided for; how could it not be a loan when it was going to have to be repaid? Who ever heard of the idea that if you sell something, you have to pay back the money which you received when you sold it? My hon. friends are obviously trying to distort the meaning of this resolution.
Another phony explanation!

You may say that it is a phony explanation but I am, after all, giving an explanation which you cannot answer. You can only try your usual smear tactics.
I am now coming to the editorial. I have described what had happened at this meeting representing the people of western Canada, that they were ready to leave it to the government after hearing from their representatives at the meeting of the various

organizations to decide how it should make provision for the advances-
What about the Rosthern resolution?

I am coming to that if you will just contain yourself in patience. I met the Rosthern executive about three weeks later. Many present felt they would like to have advances made by the wheat board through the elevator agents. I pointed out to them what had happened at this marketing conference. I had with me the very sheet I hold in my hand and I read them the resolution passed by the marketing conference. I said the reason this conference did not ask for advances to be made through the wheat board was because they received advice from pool leaders and others to the effect that it would not be a good thing for the wheat board to become involved in this matter. I suggested to our executive that as the marketing conference was not ready to ask that the wheat board become involved for fear that it might damage it and as they believed in the wheat board as much as anyone, if this was the considered opinion of some pool leaders I was inclined to pay a lot of attention to it even though at the outset I had thought it would be simpler and easier to have these advances made through the elevator agents from the wheat board. But when I heard pool leaders tell me that this might adversely affect the wheat board I did not think we should go against their advice. I said, what is the government going to do? The government will know what has happened at the conference in Saskatoon. In view of the fact that this marketing conference did not pass a resolution asking for it to be done through the wheat board, in view of the advice given by some pool leaders, I said that I was satisfied that the pool leaders before giving that advice would have been in consultation with the members of the wheat board. I said that I expected the wheat board would be giving the same advice, that they should not be involved in this matter. So I said that as far as our executive was concerned I would suggest that we ask the government to take action as quickly as possible to provide advances being made to the farmer in a way that they thought would be best for the farmer and best for the wheat board.
I explained the thing just as carefully as I am explaining it to this committee. On the strength of my explanation the executive said that they thought I was right in my attitude and that I should draw up a resolution asking the government to provide for advances in such a way as they saw fit, but that I should emphasize the necessity of

those advances being made as quickly as possible because it had been suggested that the government could not provide for advances through the banks or in any other way unless they called parliament together. They said that I should ask the government to act as quickly as possible without waiting to call parliament. That was their attitude.
So I drew up this resolution asking the government to make advances against grain stored on the farm. Because I knew of the advice the government was likely to get from the pool leaders from what they had said at this conference I thought the best thing for me to do was to stress the need for early action and to ask the government to make advances without telling them how to provide for advances. The resolution reads:
Recognizing the urgent pressing need of the farmers for cash to pay outstanding bills for harvesting and other expenses and for food, clothing and fuel before the onset of winter the Rosthern federal constituency Liberal executive ask the federal government to make provision at an early date for cash advances to be made to farmers on grain stored on farms to the extent of up to one-half the value of grain deliveries expected to be made during the current crop year.
That telegram was drafted to ask the government to make advances in such a way as it saw fit. It did not ask that those advances be made through the wheat board.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

The hon. member can ask it after I am through. That is the resolution which was passed after a full explanation to the executive. Naturally when I am accused of taking one stand in the west and another stand-
Hear, hear.
My hon. friend says, "Hear, hear", but he knows that what I say now is true, that I did not take another stand. I have proved that to him.

Prove it to the
newspapers.

It may be hard to prove to them, but I think I can prove it to them if I have proved it to you. Fifty people attended and heard my explanation. They heard me say that the government was almost sure to act on the advice of the pool leaders and the wheat board because I said the fundamental policy of the Liberal government was not to interfere in any way with the successful functioning of the wheat board. I said that I was satisfied that if they were getting that advice they would set up some system of advances to be made through the banks.
Grain
I explained in the speech I made in this house that that was what had happened at the farm marketing conference.
I want to say to the members of this committee that I am not one who pretends that everything the government of this country does is in accord with what I might like to see done. We are a large country and no one part of the country can dictate the whole national policy. We have to have a national program and the majority must rule. An attempt must be made to take care fairly of all parts of the country. When the government lays down a policy which I think is the best policy for the country as a whole, 1 will support that. I know that some eastern members will support this particular measure although they may get into trouble with their constituents for doing so. It is a national policy and I must support the government that puts into effect policies with which I agree.
I am not ashamed to say that in that connection I follow the party lead. This government has set up the wheat board and it is standing solidly behind it in the midst of this crisis and that policy should have the support of every person in western Canada who believes in the wheat board.
My hon. friends say that these attacks do not have any effect on the situation. I grant that if we had an open market and wheat was always available speeches would not affect prices, but when you have over 800 million bushels of wheat under the control of the wheat board, a government body, and then there is a concerted attack being made upon the government that that board is not doing a good job in selling wheat, that it should reduce prices to get rid of the wheat, possible buyers know that the only thing necessary to be done in order to get cheaper wheat is to have the wheat board waver in its policy, for the government to tell the wheat board that they had better bow to the attacks of the opposition and drop their prices.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I must advise the hon. member that his time has expired. For his information, may I say that I have allowed him some 90 seconds for interruptions.
I knew you would never get to the wheat board resolutions.
If you will allow me to go on I will.

Mr. Chairman, I would be the first to admit that we do not grow wheat in Broadview, but last summer I had the opportunity to travel through the western part of this country and I talked to a number of

Grain
elevator operators and wheat farmers. I found that they had quite a problem before them. Listening to the minister this morning I could hardly believe my ears because according to him there does not seem to be a problem. According to the minister, the government is selling our wheat, the farmers are absolutely satisfied and everything is perfectly satisfactory.
So I phoned up the bureau of statistics at noon just to see what our selling efforts had been as compared with those of our competitors. I got figures from the dominion bureau of statistics for the last two crop years and for the first quarter of the present crop year as compared with the first quarter of the last crop year.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Is the hon. member referring to sales or exports?
I am referring to export sales; that is what they gave me.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The bureau of statistics have no record of sales; they have a record of exports.
It is the actual sales that we made expressed in millions of bushels.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It must be exports.
We will call them exports, but I understood they were export sales. They were sales that were made. We shipped the wheat out of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I think my hon. friend should be sure of what he is talking about. Sales are recorded only by the wheat board but exports are a matter of record with the bureau of statistics.

All right, I will accept the minister's correction. These are exports of wheat, and wheat flour in terms of wheat, expressed in millions of bushels. Now, I know that the minister will claim that it is not fair to compare our performance with that of the United States and Argentina because United States exports to a certain extent are giveaway exports. I know that the Argentine enters into barter deals with other countries. The minister would claim that we do not want to enter into barter deals of that kind.
Even though the United States has exported 30-8 per cent more in the last crop year than the year before, and the Argentine 21-9 per cent more, we shall not hold that against the government because that is on a different basis from that on which we deal. However, I checked with the officials of his department who are in charge of our sales, with respect to exports made by Australia and France. They have assured me that both Australia

and France sell under the same kind of competitive conditions as Canada, and that it is fair to compare our performance to the performances of those two countries. I am glad the minister agrees.
The figures I got for Canada were that in the crop year 1953-54 we exported 255-1 million bushels, and in the last crop year,
1954-55, we exported 251-8 million bushels, or a decrease of 3-3 million bushels, which is a percentage decrease of 1-3 per cent. Australia in the crop year 1953-54 exported 63-4 million bushels, and in the crop year 1954-55 exported 94-2 million bushels, or an increase of 30-8 million bushels, which is a percentage increase of 48-6 per cent. France in the crop year 1953-54 exported 34 million bushels, and in the crop year 1954-55 exported 83-8 million bushels, or an increase of 50 million bushels over the previous crop year, which is a percentage increase of 250 per cent.
Now let us look at the comparison between the first quarter of the present crop year and the first quarter of the previous crop year. In the first quarter of the previous crop year, 1954-55, Canada exported 73-8 million bushels, and in the first quarter of the present crop year, 1955-56, we exported 59-6 million bushels, or a decrease of 14-2 million bushels, which is a percentage decrease of 19 per cent. Australia exported in the first quarter of the 1954-55 crop year 21-5 million bushels, and in the first quarter of the 195556 crop year 23-2 million bushels, or an increase of 1-7 million bushels, which is a percentage increase of approximately eight per cent. France exported in the first quarter of the 1954-55 crop year 10-2 million bushels, and in the first quarter of the present crop year 16 [DOT] 1 million bushels, or an increase of 5-9 million bushels, which is a percentage increase of 58 per cent.
As I have said, I believe the minister will agree it is perfectly fair to compare the performances of France and Australia with that of Canada, as all three of us are selling under the same competitive conditions. Yet in the past crop year we exported 3-3 million bushels less than in the previous crop year, whilst the other two countries between them exported 80-8 million bushels more than they did in the previous crop year.
The same performance took place in the first quarter of this crop year. Canada dropped by 14-2 million bushels, and the other two between them have increased by approximately 7 * 6 million bushels.
That shows that our selling effort is not what should be expected of this government. Other countries working under the same competitive conditions as Canada have sold considerably more wheat during the Dast crop

year than in the previous crop year, and that
increase has been maintained into the first quarter of the present crop year. This shows that somewhere Canada is falling down. We are not as aggressive or for some other reason we are not making the sales. We are selling less wheat, whilst other countries working under the same conditions are selling more wheat.
Therefore the government is very much to be condemned for allowing competitors to beat us right across the board while our sales are dropping off. That is the kind of performance that would cause a sales manager to require a very good explanation from a salesman; if it was not forthcoming, the salesman would be out of a job. The Canadian people, especially the wheat farmers of Canada, have a right to demand an explanation for that very poor showing from this government.
The other thing that impressed me when I listened to the minister this morning was that it seemed, according to him, that the western wheat farmers are perfectly satisfied, first of all, with the selling efforts of the government and, secondly, with the bank loans which have been arranged by the government for them at 5 per cent. The best way to find out what the people think about something is first of all to go out and talk to them, which I did this fall, and secondly to have a report of a meeting where a representative group gathers and expresses its opinions. That I have here in my hand.
This is a report given of a meeting held in Minnedosa, Manitoba, in the middle of November, attended by no less a person than the genial Minister of Justice. According to this report, it was quite a meeting. As the Minister of Justice will assure the Minister of Trade and Commerce, you would not find anywhere a finer group of people than you find in Minnedosa. I had the privilege of being there last summer and the year before and I talked to many of these people. I am sure the Minister of Justice will back me up when I say that these people are good wheat farmers. This is an average wheat farming community in western Canada, and the people who live in that community and who attended this meeting-I am sure the Minister of Justice will correct me if he does not agree completely with what I say-the people who attended this particular meeting in large numbers were some of the finest people you would find. They are fair-minded, they are calm, collected, reasonable people, wanting only a square deal and asking nothing special from anybody. All that they ask is fair treatment.
Grain
They used to vote for the government.

This report I have here which appears in the Minnedosa Tribune of Thursday, November 17, is headed "Garson Gets 'Hot Potato'; Western Farmers Hostile." It states:
The honourable Stewart Garson (Minister of Justice, Lib. M.P. Marquette) had hold of a hot one on Thursday night when he stood on the stage of the Legion hall in Minnedosa following the presentation of the brief and his talk to the audience.
For a period of three hours Mr. Garson parried questions hurled at him from the floor. Although, to the casual observer, these questions may have appeared to be merely a means to trip up the cabinet minister, they were questions of vital concern to the farmers of Minnedosa area as well as the farmers across western Canada.
One of the questions that came up continually was that Canada seems to be so critical of U.S. grain selling program, but what has the Canadian government to offer in its place?
Mr. Garson said that Canada hasn't any program that she can lay her finger on at the present time.
Then I go on to a little later in the meeting and the report has this to say:
Mr. Rudolph Usick took the floor again and reiterated that as yet Mr. Garson hadn't answered the question of what was going to happen. He read from various news clippings indicating that there was a solution to the problem if the government wished to look for it.
Mr. Garson remarked that Mr. Usick should be on the wheat board at an attractive salary if he knew the answers. He asked Mr. Usick if he thought the wheat board hadn't studied all these proposed solutions. The wheat board has proven in the past that it can get rid of the grain. Unfortunately it is bucking the American giveaway program. But if the farmers will only have patience and not make the situation worse then something will turn up. Mr. Garson again admitted that there was no solution at the present time but feels that with Mr. Howe at the head things will turn out all right.
That is the kind of answer that was provided to the questions which these people were very rightly asking. A little later in the meeting the newspaper report has this to say:
Spokesmen for the farmers ridiculed the farm loan which got great approval from the audience. Mr. Garson was asked how he would like to go to the bank and borrow his salary at 5 per cent interest.
That is a very good question and I should like to hear the answer.
He would certainly have a lot of interest to pay.

I continue:
In the eyes of the farmer that is what it amounts to. He has to pay interest on his year's labour. Herbie Schulz said that there was no criticism of the wheat board but that the present crisis was the direct result of government bungling. The government has tied the wheat board up in a straight jacket as far as invoking any system that

Grain
will move grain. He said that the Canadian government is going all out at every turn-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: On a point of order, is it in order for an hon. member to read the expressions of people outside the house and, more than that, is it in order to read pages of a newspaper in a debate of this kind?
The cabinet does it all the time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On the point of order raised by the minister, I do not think there is any question that the editorial does not conflict with the rules of the house in that it does not comment on the proceedings of the house. But there is, as I think the hon. member for Broadview will agreee, if not a provision at least a series of Speakers' rulings against the reading of lengthy editorials so that the speech becomes the speech of the writer of the newspaper article rather than that of the member who has the floor. I think the hon. member is quite capable of expressing his views in his own words without too much assistance from newspapers.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. This is not an editorial. This is simply a straight news report, and I am almost through. The reason I am reading it is that I think it expresses very clearly to the house the feelings of the average wheat farmer about what the government is doing and not doing. It is for that reason and that reason alone that I am reading it, and I will be through very shortly. The report goes on to say:
With regard to the cash loans he said it was an insult to the integrity and industry of the Canadian farmer. Another young farmer wanted to know what he was supposed to do come spring. The cash loan is based on the amount of bushels of grain one has. He figures he could borrow $1,300. When he sells his grain, one-half of this goes back to the bank, leaving him a surplus of $650 which is debt. How does the government expect him to live and put in a crop on that?
That again is a very good question, and again it remained unanswered by the minister. The report continues:
These types of questions carried on until 1.00 a.m. before the 600 audience that packed the hall.
I read that, Mr. Chairman, simply to show how good, sensible, reasonable Canadian western wheat farmers feel about what the government is doing and is not doing. They are incensed about what the government is doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: What is your opinion? You are talking about sensible people but we would like to hear your view as well.

They consider it an insult. They do not consider what the government is doing

to be in any way satisfactory, and for that reason members of this house have a perfect right to stand up and demand that the government not only sell our wheat but also that until they have sold it they make available cash advances without interest to the farmers who are being victimized by the government's complete failure to sell our wheat at the present time. There is no excuse for the government not selling it. Other countries working under exactly the same competitive conditions have been able to go out and make very important increases in sales in the past year. The reason the government has not done so is that they seem to have lost their knack of selling, if they ever had it, and it is about time they took some lessons in how to sell, got out and sold and helped the farmers instead of sitting back and doing nothing about it. I certainly hope the minister will do just that.

Mr. Chairman, I think we all witnessed a very amazing performance a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Rosthern. It seems a very strange thing to me that all of a sudden the hon. member has blossomed out as the great champion of the government so far as this legislation is concerned. I do not know how to account for this thawing-out process, but I can assure the house that when this issue was being debated throughout western Canada last fall the hon. member for Rosthern and his colleagues in the Liberal party in Saskatchewan were in a deep freeze out there and we did not hear very much from them. I am not too sure whether or not it is the warm weather down there that has been a contributing factor in that thawing-out process.
