On a question of privilege, the hon. member for Assiniboia can tell my hon. friend that there was no concealment of my views because the hon. member for Assiniboia and I had a debate on the matter before the students of the University of Saskatchewan and there was no attempt to conceal my position at that time.
It was as transparent then as it is now.

I heard the speech and I did not think it was even worth considering at this point. I suppose I should rise with some temerity to take part in this debate in view of the pointed threat made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this morning to the effect that debate on this legislation should not be carried on by the opposition for any length of time. I should like to say at the outset that I am not only taking part in the debate to express my own objections to the legislation but I am also taking part at

the express request of the many thousands of farmers who reside in my constituency and who have made it known to me in no uncertain terms that I am to put forward their objections to the legislation at every opportunity.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Are you going to vote against it?

The resolution before the house, which will of course ultimately become government legislation, is the answer the government has given to the very real and critical problem which the farmers of western Canada are grappling with today. That problem is the shortage of cash brought about because of their inability to market grain and grain products. There are a good many reasons for this shortage of cash, not the least of which is their inability to market their grain products.
I am not going to take the time of the house to place on the record once again all the reasons which have already been placed there so ably by opposition members during the throne speech debate why farmers find themselves in their present position, but may I say I think there is something very sinister in this piece of legislation, something we do not see on the surface of it. This legislation confirms a suspicion widely held on the prairies that a very peculiar situation is arising in this country. That suspicion is that the government has lost touch and has lost interest in what is happening to that section of Canada. If this situation is going to continue it will in the end spell disaster for the future economy of this country. Apparently this government-and this is the view widely held in western Canada-has become obsessed with the idea that almost overnight we have blossomed into an industrial nation and that our economic prosperity in this country is no longer dependent on our agricultural industry. As a matter of fact, in so far as western agriculture is concerned, they view it as a sort of necessary evil, an embarrassment, and one for which this government is obliged continually to apologize to the rest of Canada. This resolution goes a long way towards confirming that suspicion which is held by so many people in western Canada, and I think it is disastrous.
Prior to the introduction of this legislation meetings were held in virtually every school-house and community hall in western Canada in an effort to bring to the attention of this government the fact that a serious situation had developed and that something must be done to restore to farmers in western Canada the purchasing power which they had lost. They asked for cash advances as the only reasonable and feasible method by which
Grain
that purchasing power could be restored. While I admit-as do most people out there- that the government has lost touch, I should like to take a few moments to review some of the events-and only briefly-that finally led this government to acknowledge that there was a problem in western Canada. Certainly I am not going to burden the house with an account of the dramatic part that was played by the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan. The part he played had all the ingredients of a mystery thriller. I refer to his safari to Ottawa-and the cloud of mystery that surrounded that trip-with his little black bag under his arm in which was deposited his secret formula.
Like the socialists' trip to Washington.

I am glad to note that the hon. member also has become quite vocal on this question. We are going to look forward to a speech by the hon. member for Maple Creek, knowing before he makes it that it is going to be extremely hard to listen to. I am not going to say anything about the profound pronouncement that was made by that same gentleman when he returned from Ottawa. These are things which all of us would like to forget, including the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan. The Americans have their ballad of Davy Crockett. We in Saskatchewan have the drama of Hammy McDonald. What is more important are the visits-and the statements that arose out of those visits- by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture. They were like Caesar. They went; I do not know what they saw; and they made speeches. Reluctantly they admitted that there was something wrong. As an example, the Minister of Agriculture, speaking in Edmonton, had this to say. He admitted there was something wrong but he said, "I have the answer but it is not cash advances. We need a million more people". He said that we need a greater population because we need industry but he said that we cannot get industry until we get a dam on the south Saskatchewan river. I hope the farmers of western Canada are not obliged to wait that long before some further purchasing power is returned to them.
Then we had the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he spoke to the Alberta wheat pool convention in Calgary. After making a prolonged speech he said in effect at the very end: "Farmers of western Canada, take courage. Next year you might have a crop failure." The upshot of it all was simply this. In spite of all the representations that had been made by the business and farm leaders in western Canada after they had

Grain
considered every angle of this situation and had come out in favour of cash advances, this is what happened. Instead of listening to them and taking their considered advice, this government took the advice of a sprinkling of Liberal stooges within these organizations rather than the considered opinion of these people who truly represent the farmers and the business men of western Canada.
Then when this legislation was being proposed; when we knew that this was what we were going to get; when we knew that the government as going to reintroduce the 1951 legislation which is sometimes referred to as the agricultural interim financing act, we had once again another series of meetings, this time protesting the so-called bank legislation which was being introduced. I was greatly surprised and not a little shocked the other day when I heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce say to the members of the House of Commons that the business men in western Canada were carrying on some kind of conspiracy against the farmers. He said, "My, how they would like to get their hands on this money!" In other words, he was casting doubt as to the motives of business men. That is a typical Liberal trick. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce is obliged to defend this legislation by using tactics of this kind-tactics that we would expect to come from a Liberal back bencher -it is fairly evident to me that this resolution, in so far as any merit it may have, is as barren as a mule.
After all, why should not the business men in western Canada be concerned that the purchasing power of the farmers should be restored? We know that the future prosperity and the future existence of business people scattered throughout the towns of western Canada are dependent on the prosperity of the farmer. By the same token, the farmer is just as dependent on the business man. In western Canada today-as has been stated here in this chamber today-we find the business man carrying a terrific burden of debt and carrying a great many farmers because he knows that their interests are mutual. Hence when we have statements made in this chamber that a conspiracy is going on and that the end result in all probability will be the end of the wheat board, I think that is ridiculous. I think there is a conspiracy all right, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce has named the wrong people.
I would make this statement. I believe that there is going on in this country a conspiracy to wreck the wheat board and that it is being spearheaded by this Liberal government in co-operation with the Winnipeg grain exchange. I am convinced-as are a great many 
other people-that the marketing policies being advocated and carried out by this government have done more to undermine the farmers' confidence in the wheat board than have all these other things to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred. We are now confronted with this same legislation which proved to be so ineffective in 1951. Certainly assistance was needed then as the minister pointed out today in his speech. But in spite of the fact that it was needed only $626,000 out of $20 million that was guaranteed to the banks was used not because people did not need it, but for the very simple reason that they could not get it.
What is the condition of affairs today? We are in much greater need of money today than we were in 1951. In my province the cash farm income in the first 10 months of 1951 amounted to $631 million. What is it today? In the first 10 months of 1955, the cash farm income in the province of Saskatchewan was only $283 million. Of course, if you add the $21 million that was paid out in P.F.A.A. benefits, which should have been paid out the year before, then it brings it up to about $305 million, which is only half of what it was in 1951.
Let us take a look at the principle of this bill. Let us take a look at the mechanics provided for implementing the principle of this bill. Well, it is wrong on both counts. Mechanically, it is impossible to implement the provisions of this bill, and in principle it is wrong because it has no morality in it. If a comprehensive statement were to be made incorporating all the views protesting bank loans, I am sure such a statement would clearly indicate that it is a disgrace and an insult to ask farmers to pay interest on loans against their production when they have no responsibility whatever for the inadequacy of marketing policies which apparently make it impossible to sell our grain in the markets of the world. What I have said is, in substance, the preamble of a resolution presented by the federated co-operatives to this government, an organization that speaks for 150,000 farmers in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. They came out flatfooted and asked for interest-free cash advances on farm stored grain.
I have often wondered, Mr. Chairman, what would happen if at the end of a week a worker in any other industry went to the boss and said, "I want my week's pay". The man at the wicket saying "I am sorry but we did not sell as much of the products you produced last week and we cannot pay you, but I tell you what we have done. We have made arrangements with the banker on the comer and if you can answer the questions he is

going to ask you about your business and provide the necessary security he might consider giving you part of your wages but you will have to pay 5 per cent." I leave it to the imagination of members in this house as to what would happen. The worst feature of all is the fact that the farmers, after working all year and after producing what is after all the basic wealth of this country, have now to go cap in hand to the bank and ask for a loan. After expending their labour, after expending their capital, they now have to go cap in hand and ask for a loan.
Those are the arguments, Mr. Chairman, against bank loans. Those are the arguments in favour of cash advances. What about the practicability of implementing this measure? As was said this morning, there are only 350 chartered banks in the whole province of Saskatchewan. I imagine the same condition prevails in other provinces as well. There are just as many farmers who never bother with a bank as there are who do business with the bank. The banker is in an impossible position.
I should like to point this out, Mr. Chairman.
I have talked to a good many bankers in my constituency and I have yet to have one of them tell me that he has made a single loan with grain and nothing more as security. The form the farmer is asked to fill out is not the only form he is asked to sign. The banker is in an untenable position.
What is he going to do? I will tell you what he is going to do. He is going to go to the elevator agent, as many bankers are doing, and hold a conference with the elevator agent concerning the circumstances surrounding a man's farming operations before he can honestly make a loan. That is what is happening. What then is the bank doing for the 5 per cent interest? I am not even sure they are providing the form which the farmer is asked to fill out. They do not even have to collect the money. That is the argument that was used against cash advances, and why the government said cash advances were not feasible. The elevator agent should not be loaded with the responsibility of carrying out the provisions that would be necessary, yet today we find the elevator agent is doing the very thing the government said he could no do.
I should like to read into the record the provisions for repayment. I will only read part of it. Two tickets have to be made out. The first ticket, that is to the producer, should show the details of delivery and the deduction of one-half of the net proceeds payable to the bank. The second ticket, for the remaining half of the net proceeds, should be made payable to the lending bank and should be forwarded to the bank. The
Shipment of Aircraft to Middle East elevator agents in effect are now being used as the collecting agency for the chartered banks, and at no remuneration from the bank.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it five o'clock?
Progress reported.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR A REDUCTION IN RATE OF INTEREST

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Thursday, January 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Argue for the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Small Loans Act.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR A REDUCTION IN RATE OF INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in support of Bill No. 3 dealing with the proposed amendment to the Small Loans Act and to express first of all my disappointment that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance saw fit to adjourn the debate yesterday. One of the reasons given for doing so was the fact that the government is bringing forth some legislation along similar lines during the present session. However, I would remind the house that this bill was placed on the order paper last year by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I feel that a great deal of worthwhile discussion can result in a clarification of the issues before this house with respect to this legislation. The fact that the government has announced its intention to bring in legislation on this subject is in no way a guarantee that we are going to have the type of legislation which we want at this time.
I think there is no need to stress the importance of this matter in Canada today. The hon. member for Assiniboia reminded us yesterday that the amount of credit in this country has more than doubled in the past four years and that according to recent figures the amount of debt in Canada is well in excess of $2 billion.
The high interest rates charged by the small loan companies, of course, bear most heavily on the low income groups in Canada. It is quite obvious that wealthy individuals can pay cash for their purchases and if they find themselves short of cash at any given time they are able to go to the banks and borrow money at one-quarter the amount of interest charged by the small loan companies. Therefore, when we discuss this bill we are discussing a matter that comes very close to the small wage earner in this country.
I think we should for a moment examine briefly the various factors entering into the establishing of interest rates in Canada. Quite apart from the ordinary costs of doing business the profits of the loan companies play a very large part in this matter. Figures were placed on the record yesterday which showed that there had been an increase of over 1,000 per cent in the profits of companies doing business during recent years 
and certainly the small loan companies cannot argue that a reduction in the interest rate is going to force them out of business.
The small loan field is a most lucrative one and we need only listen to the commercials which they sponsor on the radio encouraging people to borrow money from "a friendly finance company" to find an indication of the great amount of effort the small loan companies exert in order to attract business. In other words, it is not a case of their doing an individual a personal favour. They spend lots of money in advertising designed to persuade people to take out loans for the obvious reason that lending money is a profitable business. Any suggestion that there might be a curtailment of credit owing to the revision of the interest act is certainly not valid.
The question of risk is another matter which we should examine closely. The inference is left that the excessive or exorbitant rates charged by small loan companies compensate for the vast amount of risk they undertake in lending money. The very fact that the small loan companies have set aside only -26 of 1 per cent to cover losses on their operations indicates that the amount of risk involved is not as great as they would have us believe. We know, moreover, that the experience of the Canadian Bank of Commerce in this field leads us to a similar conclusion since they feel that -25 per cent is quite adequate to cover any losses which they might sustain. As a matter of fact, if one looks more closely at the personal loan plan of the Canadian Bank of Commerce one finds that since the inception of the plan in 1936 until October 31, 1953, the Canadian Bank of Commerce loaned a total of $248,461,909. These figures are contained in the report of the banking and commerce committee of 1954 at page 186. The total loans written off during that period amounted to $380,378 but there was an amount subsequently collected of $157,058 which left a net loss incurred by the personal loan plan of the Canadian Bank of Commerce of $223,320 in the period 1936 to October 31, 1953.
This amounts to less than one-tenth of 1 per cent of all the money loaned during that period by the Canadian Bank of Commerce. Under those circumstances it is difficult to understand why exorbitant interest rates should be charged by the small loan companies in Canada because if one examines the risk element incurred by the Canadian Bank of Commerce and compares it with the risks involved in the small loan company field we find there is very little difference. As a matter of fact, one will recall that prior to

1954 the banks were not permitted by law to back loans by chattel - mortgages. We know that on the basis of guarantees and endorsements-and we must consider the fact that a great deal of this money was loaned during the late 1930's, during the time of the depression-the banks suffered an almost negligible loss.
Once again I am going to refer to the 1954 report of the banking and commerce committee. The committee was informed at that time that the total secured loans of the small loan companies as of December 31, 1952, comprised 70-92 per cent of the total loans made and that the unsecured loans totalled 29.08 per cent. Comparable figures for the Canadian Bank of Commerce indicate that the bank had total secured loans of 60-35 per cent and a total of 39-65 per cent unsecured loans. It is quite easy to see that the small loan companies are taking no greater risks than those taken by this chartered bank.
Under these circumstances it is extremely difficult to understand why the small loan companies in this country should be permitted to charge such excessive rates of interest. I am concerned with the effect that the lowering of interest rates for small loan companies would have on consumer finance generally throughout the country. Perhaps more goods are financed or purchased on instalments, the purchases being financed by the firms involved; but as the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) pointed out yesterday, these rates are even more excessive.
We are told of 54 per cent being charged by a large mail order house. When I heard that figure given I found it difficult to believe that that much interest could be charged, but I turned to the catalogue of a leading mail order house-whether it is Simpsons-Sears or Eaton's does not matter-and according to the table published there I find that if you buy a $20 item to be paid for at the rate of $5 per month for four months there will be a carrying charge of $2.25.
The only way to arrive at the proper rate of interest in that case is to consider the transaction as a series of $5 loans to be repaid at monthly intervals. Thus we find that at the end of the first month the purchaser pays $5; in other words, he has had the use of $5 for one month. At the end of the second month he pays another $5 and in that instance he has had the use of that $5 for two months; at the end of the third month he pays another $5 and he has had the use of that $5 for three months. When he repays the loan with the fourth $5 payment at the end of the fourth month he has had the use of that last $5 for four months. In 67509-41
Small Loans Act
reality he has borrowed $5 for ten months, and that figures out at 54 per cent interest being charged by the large mail order houses in this country.
Under those circumstances I think it is quite evident that any general reduction in interest rates in any field will have a beneficial effect upon the rates throughout the whole field of consumer finance. In other words, a reduction in the rates of interest charged by small loan companies will force other consumer credit organizations to make a downward revision in their rates.
But the vicious part of the whole set-up is the fact that the people who can least afford the burden of excessive interest charges are the people who are forced to bear them. Under this iniquitous system it is the small purchaser buying the $20 item who must pay the 54 per cent interest. If he buys a $30 item the interest rate goes down. In other words, the bigger the amount of the purchase the lower the rate of interest.
While I realize that we are not concerned in this bill with the carrying charges of large retail organizations I do suggest that the passage of the bill with the consequent reduction in the interest rates allowed to be charged in the small loans field would of necessity bring a downward revision in the whole field of consumer finance. We have to recognize the fact that credit plays and will play an important part in our economy. There are those who may argue that people should save sufficient money to make these purchases, but I invite hon. members to consider the economic consequences of pursuing that line of reasoning.
I am quite certain that the average merchant in Canada depends to a large extent upon time sales in order to sell his goods. A great many people in the low-income brackets in Canada would never be able to afford what we have come to regard as the amenities of life if they could not buy on time, or else borrow money from small loan companies in order to buy the article outright.
We have no idea of the nature of the legislation the government proposes to bring down, but I think this debate will serve a most useful purpose if hon. members are able to impress upon the government the necessity of bringing about a reduction as outlined in the bill we are now discussing. If we are going to permit the charging of excessive interest rates we must justify our action in the light of the facts. I think I have said enough this afternoon to indicate that neither the profits made by the small loan companies nor the risks involved are justification for charging a rate of 2 per cent per month on the unpaid balance.

Small Loans Act
I have not heard a cogent argument as yet as to why we should persist in forcing that rate of interest on the people of this country. In the small loans field it is the small wage earner, the little fellow, who borrows, and I think this is one way in which we as a parliament can give some measure of relief to the people who are in greatest need.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill is similar to one introduced last session by the same hon. member. I am not going to comment upon it at length as I intend to wait until the government's legislation is before the house. However, I do want to take this opportunity to make certain comments in connection with a meeting called by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in my constituency shortly before the last session of parliament ended, and at which he mentioned the Small Loans Act. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar came to Moose Jaw and held a meeting in our technical school auditorium. He made a number of charges against me, in which I know the house would not be particularly interested. Perhaps I am biased, but I felt that most of them were incorrect. There was one in particular which I should like to mention now. I should like to quote from a report of the meeting which appeared in the Regina Leader-Post as follows:
Mr. Coldwell cited Thatcher's differences of opinion and said that when the C.C.F. party attempted to introduce measures to reduce the 24 per cent interest charges of small loan companies, to 12 per cent, Mr. Thatcher was directly and emphatically opposed to such a move. He contended, according to Mr. Coldwell, that the loan companies could not operate, and people would not be able to borrow money to buy washing machines and other articles on time.
People who were at the meeting told me ;hat the hon. member went on to intimate that I was vigorously opposing this legislation, because I knew that if it passed I would not be able to sell merchandise from my hardware store.
What are the facts? I wish to say most emphatically-I have Hansard of the debate which took place-that I never commented on this particular bill at any time since I came to parliament. Page 3535 of Hansard of May 6, 1955, shows that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) introduced the bill. It was then spoken to by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) and a few days later, by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and a member from British Columbia. There was no vote taken. I say that either the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had a research assistant who did not do his homework thoroughly, and who passed on information which was

not correct, or he deliberately misrepresented the facts. If he was guilty of an error, then I would ask him publicly to apologize. If he was not, I say again that he very unfairly misrepresented the facts. This was only one of a number of charges which the hon. member made on that occasion. Later in the session I hope to refute some of the others. I say again that I think the hon. member, in coming to my constituency and taking a meeting when I was not there, should at least have stuck to the facts.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR A REDUCTION IN RATE OF INTEREST
speechtext: The house will realize that, when the hon. member referred to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and said that he had deliberately misrepresented certain facts or had unfairly made certain statements, I did not intervene, although some hon. members looked in my direction, because he was referring to words that were pronounced outside this house. I wish to state that if the statements referred to had been made in this house and if the hon. member were to use the same language, I would have immediately asked him to withdraw.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR A REDUCTION IN RATE OF INTEREST
speechtext: I am sorry if I did not make myself clear. I said that either one of two things must have happened. Either he must have been labouring under a misapprehension, in which case I would ask him publicly to apologize, or he was misrepresenting the facts. It must be one or the other. This is the newspaper clipping. If he has made an error, I would be glad to accept an apology and then the matter can be ended.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR A REDUCTION IN RATE OF INTEREST
speechtext:
There is an aspect to this proposed legislation that has not yet been touched upon, one which came to light two years ago before the banking and commerce committee. I refer now to the proceedings of that committee as set out on page 1071 of the report of those proceedings on Thursday, April 8, 1954. On that occasion the committee had been discussing the operations of the personal loan department of one of the chartered banks. The general manager of that bank was before the committee as a witness. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) asked him this question:
Q. May I ask you if the Canadian Bank of Commerce has been asked to extend loans to small loan companies since going into this operation?
That referred to the personal loan operation. The answer was:
A. We have small loan companies who borrow from us. On our books we have a number of customers.
Q. Has this operation affected the business you have done with those small loan companies who were your customers?
A. Yes.

There was a further question:
The next question was:
Q. Favourably or otherwise?
The general manager made this reply:
A. We have lost some accounts.
That particular exchange at that time brought to my attention-though I suppose it should not have been necessary-one aspect of the operations of these small loan companies that had not occurred to me, and that is that they are in effect retailers of a commodity that is wholesaled to them by the chartered banks:	the commodity of
credit. If we are to assume, as I think we have the right to assume, that these companies in all probability obtain their funds from the chartered banks at between five and six per cent or possibly at a much smaller percentage, and in return retail them at rates approaching 24 per cent, we see that the mark-up on this commodity is in the neighbourhood of 400 per cent.
I suggest that we should look very carefully into this situation. The chartered banking system of Canada holds a position in our economy that is perhaps unrivalled by the banking system of any other country. It has complete control of the operations of our commercial banking system. It has explicit and implicit protection and support from the government, and the experience of one of the chartered banks in entering into this very necessary field would seem to me to indicate that it is a field in which the chartered banks should be encouraged to enter more readily than they have done in the past.
I was particularly interested two years ago when Mr. Neil J. McKinnon of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, in making his presentation in support of the request for an amendment to permit the taking of chattel mortgages, said that at the outset of their operations in the personal loan department they had required the signatures of two guarantors for every loan. Later this was reduced to one endorser, and in recent years 40 per cent of their loans had been made without any endorsation or guarantee whatever. This would indicate that this business is a comparatively safe one for the banks to engage in. I believe we should give encouragement to the banks already officially and openly in the business and also encourage the other chartered banks to follow suit. I know of no better way to do that than to reduce the enormous mark-up, as I have described it, now charged by the private loan companies on the funds they receive from the chartered banks for their business purposes.
67509-41J
Small Loans Act
Admittedly, the operations of this particular bank in the personal loan field have not been as extensive as one might have wished and have not been as extensive, I rather gather, as the general manager himself would have wished. During the hearings of the banking and commerce committee, I had a suspicion in my mind that there had been, if not opposition, at least rather lukewarm support for this program on the part of the bank directors, because the general manager informed us he was not at all satisfied with the extent to which they had advertised this particular service. I myself remarked that I was surprised to hear of it, as I had been a customer of that bank for a number of years and I myself had never come across any advertising or any literature on the subject of their personal loan department. It was in reply to that comment Mr. McKinnon admitted that they had been in his opinion far too conservative in their program of advertising.
I think we have in this country a banking system of sufficient size, sufficient diversity and sufficient flexibility to enable it to undertake this very necessary function for the Canadian people. I would feel much happier if I knew that those who are in need of immediate short-term financial help on a small scale were able to go to the chartered banks rather than to these organizations, which presumably are quite financially sound, but which, on the other hand, are springing up all over the country and by means of their exorbitant interest rates are putting shackles around the necks of too many of our people today. So it is with great emphasis that I voice my support for this long overdue piece of legislation.

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR A REDUCTION IN RATE OF INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one idea I should like to advance, and I think only one. My hon. friend from Assiniboia has already covered the purpose of the bill. He has stated that the object of this bill is to reduce the maximum rate that may be charged by small loan companies from 24 per cent to 12 per cent.
My idea relates to the methods of advertising. In some cases they are nothing short of dishonest and vicious-and those are two words that for me are rather strong. I would point out that in the case of the wrapping of bacon we made it illegal-the Minister of * Justice will probably correct me here, but at any rate there was an understanding that those people would no longer wrap their bacon, fat or otherwise, in red tinted wrapping paper. That restriction has become effective. It is a case of what I call dishonest advertising. If that was one then certainly here is another. As a matter of fact, I do

Small Loans Act
not think I would characterize the sample I have in my hand in that way. This one is pretty decent compared with most. In fact it is rather pleasant and at the same time pathetic. It takes the form of a nice little Christmas wrapper, and everything is sweetness and light. There is the picture of a little girl cuddling her doll in front of a brightly lit Christmas tree, and they say in the advertisement:
The holiday season brings added happiness to young and old alike, but at the same time it is the season when many of us find ourselves short of cash because of extra expenses.
To state it briefly, if I had been introducing this private bill or if I were to introduce another one I would say that anyone whose business is the lending of money should be compelled to state the rate of interest per annum in his advertisement and I emphasize the words "per annum." That is the crux of the whole matter because the people who use these small loan companies, the people who get into these little financial jams, the people to whom this sort of pleasant thing appeals, are people who are not customarily very adroit in the matter of calculating the amount of interest per annum. Very often they have their backs to the wall. To use a colloquialism, they are in a jam and they have to do something about it immediately.
Perhaps if they knew what the rate of interest was they would take the money anyway in some cases, but I think the rate of interest per annum should be clearly stated. I have taken one example from this comparatively harmless table. For instance, they say that you can get $1,000 in cash by agreeing to repay $93.11 per month over a period of 12 months. That is all it says. You get $1,000 in cash and you repay $93.11 per month for 12 months. If I am correct in my calculations, at the end of the year you have paid back $1,117.32. That means that for the use of the $1,000 over the period-there is the catch, of course; what is the period-you pay $117.32. If you divide by 10 you are paying $11.73 for the use of $100.
I am quite sure that many people who have used such loans would say when approached that they had paid 11.73 per cent for the use of the money. But how does it work out? First of all you have to repay something every month. You have to pay back one-twelfth of the loan every month and so you actually only have the whole $1,000 for one month. Then over the next 11 months the amount of the loan diminishes by something less than $90 each month until you come to the final month when you have scarcely any of the company's money at all. Nevertheless in the final month you are still paying the same amount, not rate, of interest as you paid in the first month.

Therefore when I said that the matter of the period is all-important I meant just that. The situation can be put in two ways. You can say that you have the use of $1,000 for six months or you can say that you have the use of half of the money, $500, for the 12 month period. I just made a rough calculation when the debate started, but I think I am perfectly safe in saying that the interest rate is well over 20 per cent and probably approaches the legal limit of 24 per cent.

speechtext: Thank you very much. We have a mathematician in the house. At any rate, I think I have made my point. I hope that something will be included in the government legislation along the lines I have indicated. Let us face it that many of these people are ignorant and in a particular financial crisis they will turn to anyone who will provide them with some money. I say that the government or somebody should protect them against themselves. I do not say that anyone in the business of lending money should be compelled to advertise, but if he wants to advertise setting forth the amount to be paid back over a certain period and so on, then I say that he should be compelled by law to state the amount of interest per annum, and I put the emphasis on the last two words, "per annum."

maintopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR A REDUCTION IN RATE OF INTEREST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the government very much for proposing to take some action in this very difficult matter. Those who were members of the banking and commerce committee will recall that this matter came before the committee when we met at the last session to amend the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act. Of course the members of the banking and commerce committee were very interested in the subject because of various reasons with which they are as familiar as the members who have spoken. They were particularly interested in what the Canadian Bank of Commerce was doing in the matter.
However, there was a feeling in the committee revising the Bank Act that it might be unwise, when they were dealing with the revision of that act, to pass any legislation which would in any way interfere with the maximum limit the banks can charge under the Bank Act, namely, 6 per cent per annum. There was the thought that the

Canadian Bank of Commerce was doing a real public service in supplying money to borrowers of small loans at a cheaper rate than the small loan companies. There was some question as to why the other banks were not entering the field more and what could be done to assist them to enter the field in a bigger way.
As I remember it, it was finally decided that it would be unwise for us to change the maximum limit in the Bank Act from 6 per cent in order to encourage the making of these small loans by other banks because it was so hard to define a small loan, and if we lifted the maximum amount of 6 per cent the question would then arise as to how you would prevent loans now being made by the banks at 6 per cent at a higher rate than 6 per cent under any new provision that might be included in the legislation. In other words unless you could define a small loan so that a whole lot of loans made today at 6 per cent would not be made at the higher rate, then in trying to solve the problem you might bring about the result that more people would have to pay more interest than they were paying before.
I do not think anybody in the banking and commerce committee felt that any really satisfactory conclusion had been reached. It was realized that the Canadian Bank of Commerce in receiving an effective rate of interest of 10-46 per cent was, in the opinion of some lawyers, infringing on the Bank Act which sets the maximum rate a bank can collect at 6 per cent. The Canadian Bank of Commerce had received a legal opinion which indicated they had the right to operate as they were doing and they were going ahead with that business, but apparently the other banks would not enter the field unless there was some change in the Bank Act to put it beyond doubt that they had a right to charge more than the 6 per cent set out in that act.
As I have stated, the banking and commerce committee were a little bit nervous about tampering with the maximum rate and I do not think anybody really suggested that the maximum rate in the Bank Act should be changed. The Canadian Bank of Commerce was asked if they could suggest an amendment that would prevent loans being made- loans that today are being made at 6 per cent-at a higher rate of interest than 6 per cent and restricted to strictly personal loans. I think they brought in a suggested amendment but one which I believe did not satisfy any member of the banking and commerce committee. I should say I think most of the members of the committee felt really appreciative of the attitude of the Canadian Bank of Commerce because they were persisting
Small Loans Act
in staying in this field which they had entered about 18 years ago and were providing money to borrowers at less than 12 per cent a year. I expect that it is the attitude of the government to ask some committee either here or in the Senate to go into this matter. It is such a complicated matter that I would not want to express any definite opinion on it in case it is referred to our banking and commerce committee of which I am a member.
When the first small loan bills came before this house-I think it was in 1937-to authorize a rate of 2 per cent per month being charged, I opposed those bills strongly. Then evidence was brought in indicating that if you do not provide a legal way by which borrowers of small amounts can get money at 2 per cent interest, you will find that they are resorting to lenders who are not under any control whatever and who will charge more. That is the argument that was used. Finally it was accepted by the banking and commerce committee and these bills finally went through after they had been before the banking and commerce committee for two sessions.
As I say, this question again came before the banking and commerce committee last year. I think it would perhaps be useful to read the comment or the summing up of the Canadian Bank of Commerce in the matter because it is something in which I think all hon. members are greatly interested and are much concerned about, namely that persons having to borrow small sums of money should not be obliged to pay exorbitant rates for it. This comment by the Canadian Bank of Commerce in their brief indicates some of the difficulties involved in the matter. As I say, I want to commend the government for introducing legislation so that something can be done about it if it is at all possible.
I am reading from page 822 of the proceedings of the standing committee of the House of Commons on banking and commerce. This is from the brief of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. Before I read that comment I might say that the members of the committee were greatly interested in the brief because it made an examination of the small loan companies' operations and compared them with their own. An examination of their earnings and costs-that is of the personal loan plan of the Canadian Bank of Commerce -shows, as I have said, that total earnings were at the rate of 10-46 per cent upon loans outstanding; that their salaries amounted to 2-77 per cent on loans outstanding; that their advertising amounted to 0-15 per cent on loans outstanding, an extremely small amount; and that other expense, including salary costs and other expenses at branches,

Small Loans Act
amounted to 3-25 per cent on loans outstanding; and that the cost of funds was 2-05 per cent. In other words, the Canadian Bank of Commerce was providing funds for the small loans branch of their activities for 2-05 per cent. This fact indicates that they were not charging a large amount of interest for the use of those funds. In commenting on this matter here is what they said at page 819. They say:
These comparisons-
That is with the small loan companies.
-are made not to offer any commentary on the operations of the small loan companies, v/hich have obviously filled a public need in a high-cost field. The comparisons do indicate, however, that extreme economy in operations has been necessary under the personal loan plan.
That is the bank plan.
During the past 18 years the annual operating results of the personal loan plan showed a loss in each of five years and a net profit of less than $50,000 in each of six years.
That is the situation although the bank was charging an effective rate of 10-46 per cent and was getting its money for 2-05 per cent. The brief goes on to say this:
It is apparent that if expenses in the personal loan department had not been restricted to a low level compared with the small loan companies the department would have operated at a heavy loss throughout the period.
In other words the bank suggests that if they had not held down expenses to the very minimum in that branch of the bank's operations, they would have had a heavy loss throughout. They sum the whole situation up in this way, and I put it before hon. members because I think all hon. members are greatly interested in this matter and that they might well consider the opinion of this expert in the Canadian Bank of Commerce. Here is what he said:
As the personal loan plan offers facilities to the public similar to the small loan companies, but at much lower cost, it is natural to seek reasons for its failure to show greater growth. There is no single answer but the following observations suggest an explanation:
1.	The small loan companies by taking chattel mortgage security do not need to require endorsers or guarantors. This enables borrowers to preserve greater privacy about their affairs.
We provided for chattel mortgages being taken, so that observation should not apply any more, as I understand the amendment we made to the Bank Act. The second reason was this:
2.	The relatively low level of earnings under the personal loan plan has not permitted or warranted adequate advertising. For example, advertising costs of the personal loan plan in 1951 and 1952 totalled $10,679 while the outlays of the small loan companies totalled $1,360,775.
fMr. Tucker.]
I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to note that the Canadian Bank of Commerce apparently found that, although they were advancing money at less than half the cost to the borrower compared with what was charged by the small loan company, they did not get any great amount or proportion of the business and they attribute one of the reasons to the power of advertising. They said that their charges were so low that they were able to spend in two years only slightly over $10,000 while during the same time the small loan companies spent $1,360,000. It shows the power of advertising. Even although the small loan companies were . charging twice what the bank was charging, that was the situation. I think there is a great deal in what was said by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) with regard to these people doing the kind of advertising they do at the cost of the borrower. Their third observation is as follows:
3.	Part of the reason for the low level of advertising expenditure, however, derives from policy. During the period of voluntary credit restriction of 1951/1952 and in earlier years of full employment the bank did not seek to expand personal loan volume, believing that this was not, at that time, in the public interest. It is doubtful, however, whether this had much effect other than to permit a larger volume of loans to go to the small loan companies.
In other words, as I understand it, the bank is saying there that they did not think it was in the public interest to try to press these small loans at that time. But they seemed to think that because they did not do so it meant that more went to the small loan companies.
4.	The element of cost is probably not a significant consideration in the minds of the majority of small loan borrowers.
Here is the opinion of the Canadian Bank of Commerce after being 18 years in this business. In their opinion, the element of cost is probably not a significant consideration in the minds of the majority of small loan borrowers. I must admit that that to me was a most surprising thing because surely most people do not like to pay an effective rate of 24 per cent if they could get the money for 10 per cent or less. However, this is the opinion of the Canadian Bank of Commerce. Apparently good advertising can overcome the desire of people to get a good bargain.
The Canadian Bank of Commerce then winds up its statement like this:
The personal loan plan of the Canadian Bank of Commerce was created to provide a necessary service to the public at the lowest cost consistent with an economic operation; its methods of operation must, of course, conform with legal opinions upon which the scale of charges is based.

I would point out to the members that the actual situation in regard to the Canadian Bank of Commerce is that it had a net profit, after income tax, on loans outstanding of *77 per cent. In other words, they did not earn a profit of even 1 per cent on loans outstanding.
Then, they said: they could not afford to advertise. They said they could not charge any more than they were because the base of the charge was regulated by the Bank Act. They took it that act permitted them to take a discount of 6 per cent ahead of time, but they could not go beyond that. They were definitely limited by the Bank Act as to what they could do. They said:
-its methods of operation must, of course, conform with legal opinions upon which the scale of charges is based. As previously mentioned, the present basis is not sufficient to permit the necessary publicity and development in rendering service of greatest breadth, but it is not suggested, that a scale of charges approaching the level sanctioned under the Small Loans Act should be considered. Experience has shown that the personal loan plan of the Canadian Bank of Commerce can provide an effective service at lower rates and it has also shown that authority to take security in the form of chattel mortgages is a necessary condition to the providing of comprehensive personal loan facilities.
The bank suggested, as I understood them, that the personal loan plan should apply to loans up to $3,000 or $3,500. If I may summarize in my own words what I understood this brief to say, it was that if there were some change in the law to enable them to charge something more than this 10-6 per cent, then they could extend these services to a greater extent than they had heretofore. But they made it very plain that they were not asking for a rate of charges similar to those in the Small Loans Act. The banking and commerce committee found this brief of the Canadian Bank of Commerce very intriguing, and I think believed it to be the basis upon which a further investigation should be carried out as to the way in which the banks of this country could be asked, as a public service, to enter this field. After all, the banks do get very valuable rights from this parliament. At the same time, in opening this field today, they felt we should not in any way change the limit of 6 per cent on ordinary loans.
I believe all members of the house, and particularly the members of the banking and commerce committee, will agree with me that this is a very difficult problem and one upon which we were justified in not embarking in connection with our study and revision of the Bank Act. At the time I felt this brief did lay down a foundation upon which an investigation could be made to ascertain what
Small Loans Act
use could be made of the bank facilities in this country to ensure that borrowers of small amounts of money would not have to pay 24 per cent interest. I believe all members will agree that all the banks should be expected to render this service to small borrowers as part of the public service they should render in connection with the grant of their charters. At the same time, nothing should be done to interfere with the maximum amount of interest that can be charged on ordinary loans.
This is not an easy problem to solve. Certainly it is one which I think the members of this house will be glad to have an opportunity to study. My own feeling when the motion was made yesterday to adjourn this debate was that it was the thought of the parliamentary assistant (Mr. Benidickson) to the Minister of Finance that it might be a good thing if a careful study of what had happened in the past were made before various members committed themselves too definitely; that if we obtained advice from experts in this field we would not appear to be pre-judging the matter before it did come before us. It was for that reason I supported the parliamentary assistant. I believe everybody will agree this is a difficult and complicated matter. When the government has promised to introduce a bill covering the matter, I think most members of the house will want to be sure they give it the fullest possible study and get the best possible advice, in order to make sure that the course embarked upon is in the best interests of the small borrowers in this country.
